fields.result: CircLS lowers arbitrary Pauli product measurement sequences to physical Stim circuits via linear-time stabilizer construction rules with dynamic patch allocation, cutting allocated spacetime volume by 5.5x and logical error rate by 14x.
fields.question: How can Pauli product measurement sequences for lattice surgery be compiled down to fault-tolerant physical circuits and realistically verified rather than evaluated via isolated logical-level formulas?
fields.prior: Static patch allocation toolchains (DASCOT, lsqecc) emitting runnable circuits; logical error formulas deviated from physical circuit measurements by up to 6.8x.
fields.limits: Evaluated at surface code distances d from 3 to 11 under circuit-level noise rates p=5e-4 and p=1e-3, with some benchmarks restricted by decoder compute budgets or missing catalytic Y-state replay protocols.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1. (a) Lowering the PPM $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ : CircLS constructs the stabilizers that measure the product, then emits the physical circuit. (b) Under static allocation a data patch holds its tile from start to end, so it collects extra noise before its first use and after its last use. CircLS allocates the patch at its first use and frees it at its last use, and the freed span is open for ancilla path reuse. (c) and (d) Freeing shortens ancilla paths: patches 1 and 3 are jointly measured. With patch 2 still allocated, the ancilla path detours through five tiles. With patch 2 freed, it runs straight through three tiles.

fields.result: Constructs quantum CSS codes with strict transversal T on all logical qubits that achieve constant rate with growing distance, and codes with magic state distillation overhead exponent gamma -> 0.
fields.question: Can asymptotic families of quantum CSS codes with strictly transversal T gates achieve constant rate and growing distance or better polynomial rate-distance scaling?
fields.prior: Parameters unchanged since Hastings and Haah (2017) and Haah (2018); constant rate with growing distance previously unachieved even allowing Clifford corrections.
fields.limits: Asymptotic code families; analytical construction with randomized selection step.
tools: puncturing at downward-closed sets on Boolean hypercube

fields.result: Standardized benchmark suite and infrastructure (ABSTRACTS) for classical Clifford+T circuit simulators with fixed circuit dataset and standardized virtual hardware.
fields.question: How to fairly compare runtime and resource efficiency across disparate classical simulators of non-Clifford quantum circuits?
fields.prior: Simulators tested on ad-hoc, author-chosen circuits and disparate local hardware without canonical benchmarks.
fields.limits: Focuses specifically on Clifford+T / non-Clifford classical quantum circuit simulation methods.

fields.result: AshN native two-qubit gate scheme reduces two-qubit gate counts by geometric means of 45.2% (1D) and 43.7% (2D) versus CZ-based compilation across seven benchmark circuits; prepares eight-qubit two-excitation Dicke state with fidelity 0.736 and certified genuine multipartite entanglement, which fails under CZ compilation.
fields.question: Can native continuous-angle two-qubit gate engineering merge routing with logical operations to overcome sparse physical connectivity in superconducting processors?
fields.prior: Standard controlled-Z (CZ) based compilation on constrained 1D/2D lattices requires extensive SWAP routing overhead.
fields.limits: Tested on benchmark circuits up to eight qubits and 1D/2D layouts with up to three connectivity defects.

fields.result: Introduces Graphix, an open-source Python framework for compiling, optimizing, and simulating measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) protocols and pattern workflows.
fields.question: How to create a unified software library bridging theoretical MBQC formulations with standard quantum computing workflows and classical simulation tools?
fields.limits: Software tool paper; performance and scale limited by backend classical quantum simulators.

fields.result: Proves unconditional security of Yamakawa-Zhandry certified randomness protocol against adversaries making up to o(\log \lambda) adaptive quantum queries to random oracle, without Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture.
fields.question: Can the Yamakawa-Zhandry certified randomness conjecture be proven unconditionally without assuming the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture?
fields.prior: Yamakawa and Zhandry (J. ACM 2024) proved security only conditionally assuming the unproven Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture.
fields.limits: Restricted to shallow quantum adversaries making at most o(\log \lambda) adaptive quantum queries to the random oracle.

fields.result: Monolayer jacutingaite (Pt2HgSe3) tunnel barrier irradiated by off-resonant circularly polarized light achieves near-perfect valley filtering (|P_v| ~ 100%) and spin polarization |P_s| ~ 70%.
fields.question: How does off-resonant circularly polarized light combined with exchange and staggered potentials control spin- and valley-resolved quantum transport in monolayer jacutingaite tunnel junctions?
fields.limits: Theoretical calculation in the off-resonant high-frequency regime; ballistically transport with step-function junction profiles.

fields.result: WSe2-NiPS3 p-n heterostructures yield circularly polarized photocurrent with spin polarization reaching 80% near Neel temperature and persisting at 30% at room temperature without external magnetic fields or ferromagnetic contacts.
fields.question: Can magnetic van der Waals heterostructures generate and spectrally control spin-polarized photocurrents without external magnetic fields or ferromagnetic contacts?
fields.limits: Spin polarization drops to 30% at room temperature; requires optical excitation via circularly polarized light under an electric field.
tools: WSe2-NiPS3 van der Waals heterostructure p-n diode

fields.result: Intervalley trions with equal electron and hole effective masses allow exact separation of center-of-mass and internal motions. Trion binding energy increases monotonically with perpendicular electric and magnetic fields, yielding strongest binding in silicene, followed by stanene and germanene.
fields.question: How do combined perpendicular electric and magnetic fields influence the center-of-mass and internal dynamics of intervalley trions in buckled 2D Xene monolayers?
fields.limits: Theoretical/numerical calculation only, assumes equal electron and hole effective masses for exact center-of-mass separation, high-magnetic-field regime.

fields.result: Derives a statistical learning theory with a noise-order purity parameter explaining finite-noise optima via competition between reduced generalization gap (lower model complexity) and increased prediction bias. Shows the finite-noise optimum depends on learning setup and can vanish in the large-sample limit.
fields.question: How do microscopic noise processes dictate macroscopic learning performance and produce non-monotonic generalization error with a finite-noise optimum?
fields.limits: Analyzed via surrogate model; finite-noise optimum can disappear in the large-sample limit.

fields.result: Observed coherent electron spin exchange dynamics between Rydberg atoms driven by spin-orbit coupling via second-order dipole perturbation. Validated anisotropic XXZ spin dynamics in 1D chains and demonstrated interaction tuning via magnetic fields and microwave dressing.
fields.question: Can direct electron spin-spin interactions between Rydberg atoms be observed and engineered for quantum simulation?
fields.limits: Demonstrated in 1D atomic chains under applied magnetic fields and microwave fields.

fields.result: Real-time decoding stack executed on 12 cores of a single Apple M4 Max CPU decodes up to 408 logical qubits across >1,000,000 logical gates with decoding delay computation stretch <0.3% at p_CNOT = 10^-4 and <12% at p_CNOT = 5 * 10^-4.
fields.question: Can an end-to-end decoding stack perform real-time error correction and dynamic detector error model generation for universal fault-tolerant quantum computing at MegaQuOp scale using a single CPU?
fields.prior: Streaming decoding was demonstrated for 15 logical qubits with 27 logical measurements, and for 100 distance-5 surface codes using an FPGA network.
fields.limits: Circuit-level noise model with noisy syndrome extraction and cat measurements; assumes 1 ms/SEC for 102 logical qubits and 5 ms/SEC for 408 logical qubits; physical noise rate p_CNOT from 10^-4 to 5 * 10^-4.
tools: Dual sliding-window decoder (error and outcome decoders)
Single 2024 Apple M4 Max CPU (12 cores)

fields.result: Flag fault-tolerant preparation of logical |√T⟩ magic states on the 3D tetrahedral color code and morphed variant reduces the average space-time cost of synthesizing Haar-random single-qubit unitaries by ~20-30% relative to Clifford+T.
fields.question: Can fault-tolerant |√T⟩ magic state preparation and injection be realized efficiently enough to reduce quantum circuit synthesis overhead compared to standard Clifford+T synthesis?
fields.prior: Clifford+T gate set magic state distillation and synthesis.
fields.limits: Evaluated under circuit-level noise simulations; applies to single-qubit Haar-random unitaries in early fault-tolerant regimes.

fields.result: Encoding noise-biased qubits in Fock states |0> and |n> with engineered dissipation achieves bit-flip probabilities approaching 10⁻⁸ for controlled-X gates at n >= 9, reaching repetition-code logical error rates of p_L* = 10⁻⁶ at code distance d = 9.
fields.question: Can non-biased ancilla transmon back-action errors during syndrome extraction be prevented without the complex Hamiltonian engineering required for all-cat bias-preserving gates?
fields.limits: Numerical simulations; assumes odd n, engineered dissipation rate much larger than intrinsic rates (κ_s >> κ_i), and rotating-wave approximation conditions on filter detunings.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Average logical error per round $p_{L}^{*}$ when the 0-n Fock qubit is used as an ancilla in the repetition code, paired with cat data qubits. The contours for $p_{L}^{*}\in\{10^{-4},10^{-5},10^{-6}\}$ are shown as a function of $\kappa_{1}T_{\text{cycle}}$ and the code distance $d$ , where $\kappa_{1}$ is the single-photon loss rate of the cat qubits, and $T_{\text{cycle}}$ is the cycle time for a single round of error correction. We work with a phenomenological noise model, where $Z$ errors are applied on the ancilla and the data qubits at the start of each error correction round. The ancilla $Z$ errors occur only due to single-photon events ( $\tau_{i}^{\downarrow}=250\;\mu\text{s},\,\tau_{i}^{\uparrow}=250$ ms) during the stabilization ( $t_{s}=500$ ns), or the CX gates ( $t_{g}=200$ ns): we assume large enough $E_{J}/E_{C}$ such that dephasing due to charge noise is sufficiently suppressed. Lastly, the cat qubits have a mean photon number of $|\alpha|^{2}=10$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Average logical error per round p_L* as a function of the single-photon loss rate product κ_1 T_cycle and repetition code distance d, showing the threshold for megaquop performance (p_L* = 10⁻⁶) at d = 9.

fields.result: Identified index-order, missing Kronecker delta ($\delta_{j_N,k_N}$), and conjugation errors in proof of Theorem 1 in Schuld (arXiv:2101.11020v2) Appendix A; provided exact corrected Fourier expansion for quantum kernels.
fields.question: Are the explicit Fourier coefficient derivations for quantum kernels in Appendix A of Schuld (2021) mathematically correct?
fields.prior: Derivation in Schuld (2021, arXiv:2101.11020v2) had reversed index ordering, missing overlap deltas, and swapped conjugate labels in explicit Fourier expressions.
fields.limits: Purely analytical correction. Does not alter the validity of Theorem 1 itself.

fields.result: Optimal fidelity for purifying an unknown $d$-dimensional unitary under depolarizing noise $p$ scales as $F = 1 - \frac{(d^2-1)(d^2+2)}{4d^2n}p + O(n^{-2}p, p^2)$, achievable via an $\mathrm{SU}(d)$-covariant parallel strategy.
fields.question: What is the fundamental limit of fidelity for purifying an unknown $d$-dimensional unitary channel from $n$ noisy uses under depolarizing noise?
fields.prior: Known only for $d=2, n=3$ parallel protocols and as a leading-order bound for $d=2$.
fields.limits: Depolarizing noise model; asymptotic low-noise limit ($p\to 0$) and large-query limit ($n\to\infty$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: In the above figure, $J_{\alpha}$ is the basis transformation implementing the isomorphism $\mathbb{C}^{d}\simeq\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}$ , $U_{\mathrm{Sch}}$ denotes the quantum Schur transform [ 49 , 50 , 51 ] , $|\Phi_{m_{\alpha}}^{+}\rangle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_{\alpha}}}\sum_{s_{\alpha}=1}^{m_{\alpha}}|s_{\alpha}\rangle_{\mathcal{S}_{\alpha}}\otimes|s_{\alpha}\to\hat{\lambda}\rangle_{E}$ is a maximally entangled state between the Specht module $\mathcal{S}_{\alpha}$ and the environment, $V_{\eta}$ is an isometry, and $\mathrm{CG}$ denotes the Clebsch-Gordan transformation. See Appendix for details.
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit implementation of the optimal $\mathrm{SU}(d)$-covariant parallel purification protocol using quantum Schur and Clebsch-Gordan transforms on $n$ noisy channel queries.

fields.result: Derandomized classical shadow measurement achieves up to a 28.79× reduction in measurement shots over standard qubit-wise commuting (QWC) grouping for 10-qubit Heisenberg circuits with 36 initial observables, whereas direct QWC measurement requires fewer shots (0.35× to 0.02× the measurements) on larger or deeper circuits (40-qubit Heisenberg, 26-qubit Ising, 18-qubit QFT).
fields.question: How can operator backpropagation be integrated with advanced measurement protocols to minimize total measurement shots while maintaining a target accuracy?
fields.prior: Operator backpropagation (OBP) paired exclusively with qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group measurements.
fields.limits: Evaluated on classical simulations with up to 40 qubits, max error per slice of 0.0001 for backpropagation truncation, and two-qubit Pauli observables.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3 : Operator Backpropagation-Derandomization Protocol Results on a XYZ Heisenberg Hamiltonian Circuit.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots estimation error versus measurement shot count for 10-qubit Heisenberg circuits. Derandomized shadow protocols achieve lower error at fixed shot budgets compared to standard and weighted QWC operator backpropagation as observable count increases.

fields.result: Universal expectation-value sign margin for the complete quadratic-Majorana relaxation on n qubits is exactly Δ_Maj(n) = tan(π / (4n)) = Θ(1/n). For arbitrary designated binary observables on n qubits encoding m variables, the universal margin is at most √(2 ln 2 n/m).
fields.question: What physical and information-theoretic resource tradeoffs are required when classical optimization variables are compressed into quantum expectation values on fewer qubits?
fields.limits: Worst-case 1/n scaling applies specifically to the complete quadratic-Majorana observable family; uniformly random sign assignments achieve Θ(1/√ n). Information-theoretic bounds assume a fixed family of binary observables.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Three levels of compression limits. Majorana-specific. The exact result gives a $\Theta(n^{-1})$ universal worst-case margin despite $\Theta(n^{-1/2})$ typical behavior, together with a Gaussian-complete set of attainable two-point correlations (the covariance body). Designated observables. Standard QRAC information theory bounds the universal margin for fixed binary observables. Arbitrary random-access codes. Nayak’s bound converts width reduction into a copy cost for reliable recovery.
fields.figure_gloss: Three complementary bounds on quantum optimization variable compression: the exact Θ(1/n) universal margin for quadratic Majorana encodings, the √(2 ln 2 n/m) QRAC baseline for fixed observables, and the nN = Ω(m) copy-width bound for arbitrary random-access decoding.

fields.result: Proposes a switchable heavy-hole/light-hole spin qubit in a bilayer Ge heterostructure with SiGeSn barriers, showing a charge-noise sweet spot with Rabi frequencies around 100 MHz and a dephasing time of T2* = 217.6 μs.
fields.question: Can a heterostructure combine the fast spin-orbit driving of light holes with the long coherence of heavy holes in a single, gate-switchable spin qubit?
fields.limits: Theoretical simulation assuming zero hyperfine interaction (pure spin-zero isotopes), an approximate continuous compositional profile (sigma = 0.8 nm), and Ge Luttinger parameters across the entire heterostructure.
tools: bilayer Ge heterostructure with unstrained Si0.50Ge0.35Sn0.15 barriers
fields.figure_caption: Figure 14: Calculated dephasing time as a function of plunger gate voltage. The barrier width is $d=3$ nm, the confinement frequencies are $\hbar\omega_{x}=2$ meV and $\hbar\omega_{y}=2.6$ meV. (a) The dephasing time is calculated using Eqs. ( 18 ), ( 22 ) and ( 24 ), assuming an infrared cutoff frequency $\omega_{\mathrm{ir}}/2\pi=10^{-2}$ Hz and $\sigma(t=1\hskip 2.84526pt\mu\mathrm{s})=10$ $\mu$ V. The magnetic field is along $y$ , $B_{y}=0.1$ T. Two peaks appear close to the HH-LH resonance. (b) Detailed view of the two dephasing time peaks shown in (a). (c) Corresponding effective $g$ -factor as a function of gate voltage. The dashed lines show the positions of the dephasing time peaks shown in (a) and (b).
fields.figure_gloss: Calculated dephasing time T2* (a, b) and effective g-factor (c) versus plunger gate voltage Vg. Shows first-order charge-noise sweet spots near the heavy-hole/light-hole resonance where T2* peaks above 200 μs.

fields.result: Realized noise-biased qubit using single microwave pump on standard transmon in |g>-|f> basis. Achieves order-of-magnitude relaxation time enhancement over conventional |g>-|e> encoding while losing only a factor of two in echo coherence time.
fields.question: Can noise bias be engineered in a simple qubit platform while remaining compatible with fast and high-fidelity operations?
fields.prior: Conventional |g>-|e> transmon had T1^e = 133.6 μs, T2^ge = 107.2 μs, and T2E^ge = 138 μs in the same device.
fields.limits: Simulations omit dephasing noise and thermal excitations; engineered gain modelled as single-rate Lindblad dissipator rather than frequency-dependent cavity response.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Relaxation and coherence times of the gain-engineered transmon as a function of engineered gain rate $g_{\mathrm{gain}}$ . a, Pulse sequence for $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}$ measurements in c , d . The white fill in the $\pi_{\mathrm{gf}}$ pulse indicates its use for the $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}$ measurement only. b, Pulse sequence for $T_{2}^{\mathrm{gf}}$ and $T_{2\mathrm{E}}^{\mathrm{gf}}$ measurements in e , f . The white fill in the $\pi_{\mathrm{gf}}$ pulse indicates that it is used only for the $T_{2\mathrm{E}}^{\mathrm{gf}}$ measurement. c, Decay times $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}$ ( $T_{1}^{\mathrm{g}}$ ) out of the $\left|\mathrm{f}\right\rangle$ ( $\left|\mathrm{g}\right\rangle$ ) state as a function of $g_{\mathrm{gain}}$ . The $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}$ begins to saturate at $g_{\mathrm{gain}}/2\pi=$133\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$$ ( $\kappa_{\mathrm{gain}}/2\pi=$165\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$$ ), which we indicate by the dotted gray box. The solid light green line (dashed dark green line) is a numerical simulation of $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}$ ( $T_{1}^{\mathrm{g}}$ ) with experimentally measured parameters, while the dotted black line is an analytical theory prediction derived from the multilevel transmon decoherence model (Eq. ( 3 )). Note that $T_{1}^{\mathrm{g}}$ for the lowest $g_{\mathrm{gain}}$ values is omitted because the measurement contrast is too low to extract a decay time. d, Relaxation measurement traces for $g_{\mathrm{gain}}/2\pi=$133\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$$ . Circles (diamonds) are data for the $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}$ ( $T_{1}^{\mathrm{g}}$ ) measurement, and the solid line is a simple exponential fit which yields $T_{1}^{\mathrm{f}}=$2.22(\pm 0.06)\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$$ ( $T_{1}^{\mathrm{g}}=$1.67(\pm 0.34)\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$$ ). e, Ramsey coherence time $T_{2}^{\mathrm{gf}}$ (dark blue circles) and echo coherence time $T_{2\mathrm{E}}^{\mathrm{gf}}$ (light blue diamonds) as a function of $g_{\mathrm{gain}}$ . f, Echo measurement trace for $g_{\mathrm{gain}}/2\pi=$133\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$$ . Circles are data and solid line is a fit (see Supplementary Information Sec.. III.C), which yields $T_{2\mathrm{E}}^{\mathrm{gf}}=$65(\pm 4)\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s}$$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Relaxation and coherence times as a function of engineered gain rate g_gain. Shows enhancement in relaxation time alongside changes in coherence times.

fields.result: Tensile-strained SiGe quantum wells lattice-matched to Ge host light-hole spin qubits with transition dipole moments three orders of magnitude larger and quality factors an order of magnitude higher than conventional strained-Ge heavy-hole qubits.
fields.question: Can a light-hole ground state spin qubit be engineered using only SiGe heterostructures lattice-matched to a Ge substrate without metamorphic buffers or Sn integration?
fields.prior: Conventional strained-Ge heavy-hole qubits on metamorphic SiGe buffers suffer from large g-tensor anisotropy (g*_|| ≈ 0.1, g*_⊥ ≈ 15) and substrate-induced dislocation noise.
fields.limits: Purely theoretical and numerical simulation; noise analysis assumes charge noise is dominated by vertical electric field fluctuations with fixed amplitude 10 kV/m.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) Computed dipole moment as the transition matrix element of the position operator between the two computational states $d=\bra{0}x\ket{1}$ , expressed in nm, for a planar confinement $L_{X_{0}}=35$ nm, barrier composition $\text{Si}_{70}\text{Ge}_{30}$ , vertical electric field $F_{z}=1.2$ MV/m and magnetic field amplitude $15$ mT. Overlayed in black is the dipole moment of the $\varepsilon$ -Ge HH heterostructure utilized for comparison. (b) Ratio of Quality factors $Q=T_{2}^{*}d_{\text{eff}}eE_{\text{AC}}/\hbar$ for a Light-Hole ground state in the tensile strained SiGe well ( $Q_{LH}$ ) and a $\varepsilon$ -Ge HH hole spin qubit ( $Q_{HH}$ ) computed for fluctuations around a vertical field of $1.2$ MV/m. (c)-(d) Proposed heterostructure to achieve a HH-LH bilayer for $0.25$ MV/m and $1.35$ MV/m respectively, showing the transition from HH to LH ground state. The grey insets at the top of each layer represent the Ge concentration in each SiGe alloy, with the underlying substrate not shown but kept fixed at pure Ge like the monolayer study. (e) Linear SOC parameter extracted as a function of out-of-plane electric field. Around $1.25$ MV/m we observe the sudden transition with a large boost in the strength of $\alpha$ . Finally (f) shows the evolution of the g-factor for the same parameter range with the typical anisotropy inversion expected between HH and LH ground states.
fields.figure_gloss: Dipole moment and quality factor ratio between light-hole and heavy-hole qubits versus quantum well thickness and composition, alongside electrical switching of ground-state character in a SiGe/Ge bilayer.

fields.result: Preserving $K$ logical qubits for $S$ time steps under independent erasure noise with error $\varepsilon$ requires minimum circuit size $C_{\min}(K,S,\varepsilon)=\Theta(S(K+\log(S/\varepsilon)))$. Constant relative overhead $\Theta(1)$ is impossible unless $K=\Omega(\log(S/\varepsilon))$.
fields.question: Can fault-tolerant quantum computation or quantum memory achieve constant cumulative spacetime overhead?
fields.limits: Independent erasure noise with erasure probability below Gilbert-Varshamov distance threshold $\delta_{\mathrm{GV}} \simeq 0.1100$, allowing adaptive protocols and ideal error recovery.

fields.result: Proves (1-o(1))-fidelity N-qubit GHZ state encoding in time O(\log N/N) using all-to-all 2-local Hamiltonians, saturating theoretical lower bound \Omega(\log N/N).
fields.question: How fast can high-fidelity GHZ encoding be performed using all-to-all interacting Hamiltonians?
fields.prior: was O((\log N)^2/N) with unproven non-vanishing infidelity (Yin 2025)
fields.limits: All-to-all 2-local Hamiltonians with bounded 2-qubit interactions; asymptotic large N limit.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2. Illustration of the TAT packet separation in the new protocol, which consists of the same steps as the start of the protocol from [ Yin25a ] shown in Figure 1 , but with different squeezing and rotation parameters. The parameters used for the three steps are those in the table in Section 1.3 with $a=9/20$ , $\kappa=9$ , and $M=1000$ . The red contours show the boundaries $y=\pm 1/3$ . In Step 1, we squeeze the state further than in Figure 1 , while in Step 2, we do a shorter controlled $X$ rotation. In Step 3, we squeeze a smaller amount to send the “core” of the packet past the $y=\pm 1/3$ boundaries, but not all the way to the $\pm Y$ poles. Stopping before reaching the $\pm Y$ poles lets us handle the exact solution to the continuum limit TAT evolution equations, which allows for obtaining rigorous estimates. Note that the packet densities (Husimi distributions) are shown in log scale, and so the packets in the controlled $X$ step are actually much more separated than they may appear.
fields.figure_gloss: Husimi distribution on the Dicke sphere showing the three-step packet separation sequence: deeper initial TAT squeezing, shorter controlled X rotation, and partial reverse TAT squeezing past y = \pm 1/3.

fields.result: Extracting containment and complementary-polarity relationships from minimized Boolean expressions reduces circuit control counts and qubit requirements. Transformation never increases representation-level cost measures.
fields.question: Can factorizing minimized Boolean expressions reduce executable quantum circuit costs compared to direct mapping?
fields.limits: Translation to executable circuits requires uncomputing auxiliary lines, which returns part of the resource savings.

fields.result: Algorithms with comparable median e-bit costs yield drastically different physical penalties: for example, MLFM-R and Pytket-ESD match closely in e-bit cost, but MLFM-R incurs a significantly higher circuit depth ratio while degrading gate density.
fields.question: How do distributed quantum circuit partitioning algorithms impact physical, circuit-level structural metrics beyond total entanglement cost?
fields.prior: Partitioning methods were evaluated almost exclusively on total entanglement (e-bit) cost and classical compilation runtime (Burt et al. 2023, Andrés-Martínez et al. 2019, Baker et al. 2020).
fields.limits: Results are aggregated rather than disaggregated by individual benchmark instance; instances that timed out during postprocessing conversion (600-second limit) are excluded; assumes ideal intra-QPU full connectivity.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 4 : Multidimensional evaluation of DQC partitioning overheads. The grouped box plots contrast e-bit cost, circuit depth ratio, $\Delta$ gate density, and $\Delta$ entanglement variance across partitioning methods.
fields.figure_gloss: Grouped box plots of distributed partitioning metrics across various partitioners, showing e-bit cost, circuit depth ratio, gate density delta, and entanglement variance delta.

fields.result: Estimation variance for molecular Hamiltonians does not scale monotonically with Platonic solid POVM complexity (4 to 20 effects); joint optimization of POVM orientation and weights using an MPS classical proxy state outperforms standard Pauli shadow measurements when bond dimension is sufficiently high.
fields.question: Can the overcompleteness and symmetry of Platonic-solid POVMs combined with locally optimal dual frames improve shadow estimation variance for molecular Hamiltonians?
fields.prior: Standard randomized Pauli measurement shadow tomography and locally-biased classical shadows (LBCS).
fields.limits: Numerical simulations on molecular Hamiltonians up to 16 qubits; relies on MPS proxy approximations with adequate bond dimension; tested primarily with 1-LO dual optimization during parameter search.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: RMSE for the $\text{NH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}$ molecule ( $16$ qubits) as a function of the locality parameter $k$ of the $k$ -LO duals. The three panels correspond to MPS proxy states with bond dimensions $\chi=1$ , $\chi=5$ , and $\chi=10$ , respectively. The RMSE is computed as in Eq. ( 9 ) using $R=10^{3}$ independent realizations of the experiment, each with $S=10^{3}$ measurement shots, and $k$ -LO duals obtained from a separate dataset of $S=10^{6}$ shots.
fields.figure_gloss: RMSE versus k-LO dual locality parameter k for a 16-qubit NH3 Hamiltonian across MPS proxy bond dimensions chi = 1, 5, and 10. Performance of optimized Platonic POVMs improves over randomized Pauli baselines as the classical proxy bond dimension increases.

fields.result: Trapped quasiparticles in bilayer graphene show localized charge of e/4 at filling factors nu = -5/2, -1/2, and 3/2, and e/3 at nu = 2/3.
fields.question: Can the quasiparticle charge of even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states in bilayer graphene be measured and localized via a gate-defined antidot?
fields.prior: Fabry–Pérot interferometers in bilayer graphene showed interferometric periodicity consistent with interfering e/2 quasiparticles enclosing e/4 localized charge.
fields.limits: Measured at B = 14 T and base temperatures below 50–70 mK; e/4 oscillations suppress rapidly above 50–70 mK.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Minimal-excitation oscillations at even-denominator and hole-conjugate FHQ states. a–d , Variation of the transmitted resistance oscillations $\delta R_{\mathrm{t}}$ as a function of the ADG voltage $V_{\mathrm{adg}}$ and the magnetic field $B$ for filling factors $\nu=-5/2,-1/2,2/3$ and $3/2$ respectively. For each panel, the lower light blue trace shows a line cut through the oscillations along the black dashed line indicated in the corresponding map. e–h , 2D-FFT of the oscillations with the corresponding extracted ADG ( $\Delta V$ ) and magnetic field ( $\Delta B$ ) periods for each filling factor.

fields.result: Inserting a 6 nm buried Si trapping layer into the lower SiGe barrier cuts the oxygen background in subsequent SiGe by a factor of 5 (from ~4e17 cm^-3 to 8e16 cm^-3) and increases electron mobility.
fields.question: How does oxygen reduction through heterostructure design affect transport across different carrier-density and temperature regimes in Si/SiGe quantum wells?
fields.limits: Measured on 200 mm Si(100) substrates with SiGe barriers grown at 600 °C; transport benchmarked at 1.5 K and 0.3 K on 7 devices per group.

The labels below the schematics denote the four investigated growth configurations and correspond to the color coding used in panels (b) and (c). (c) Silicon and oxygen depth profiles for structures with a $600~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ -grown Si QW, comparing samples without and with the additional Si trap layer, shown as orange and purple lines, respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Depth profile of silicon and oxygen concentrations measured by SIMS as a function of depth, showing oxygen background suppression in SiGe following an inserted 6 nm Si trapping layer.

fields.result: Connecting an SET in series with a high-kinetic-inductance TiN inductor triggers a superconducting-to-normal transition at the peak of Coulomb oscillations. Overcoupled operation theoretically improves SNR by a factor of over 350 relative to conventional rfSETs.
fields.question: Can superconducting phase-transition sensing enhance the charge sensitivity and readout speed of semiconductor spin qubits?
fields.prior: rfSET reflection coefficient change is bounded to small values (|ΔΓ|rfSET = 0.167 for Rparasitic = 20 kΩ), whereas PTSET reaches |ΔΓ| → 2.
fields.limits: Requires reducing inductor critical current (IC ≈ 33 nA achieved via 0.6 T out-of-plane magnetic field). Switching and recovery dynamics (estimated 10–100 ns) not experimentally resolved.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Circuit tuning of the PTSET. (a) Current-biased IV curve measurements of the TiN thin films taken at 0.6 T out-of plane field and $V_{GS}=1$ V, well in the on state of the transistor. A constant slope of 312 k $\Omega$ , 112 k $\Omega$ associated with the on-state resistance of the FET and 200 k $\Omega$ with drain and source low-pass filters, is removed to highlight the superconducting region. Red and blue backgrounds represent normal and superconducting states respectively. Vertical dashed lines indicate the phase transition current. (b) Drain current as a function of the gate-source and drain-source voltages, showing regions of charge stability, i.e. Coulomb diamonds. The horizontal red dashed line marks the voltage region used for panel c. No magnetic field applied. (c) Drain current versus the gate-source voltage for a Coulomb oscillation meeting the phase transition tune condition. Red and blue backgrounds represent normal and superconducting states, respectively. The horizontal dashed line indicates the phase transition current. (d) Change in reflected rf power versus frequency for different drain currents performed at 0.6 T out-of plane field. The background is taken at $I_{D}=0$ nA.
