fields.result: Crossed Andreev reflection achieves 100% probability ($P_{\text{CAR}}=1$) at flux $\phi=\pi$. Nonlocal differential conductance reaches $G_{RL}=-2e^{2}/h$.
fields.question: Can crossed Andreev reflection be isolated with 100% efficiency without using exotic topological materials?
fields.limits: Requires magnetic flux $\phi=\pi$, tuned junction hopping $t' \simeq t/\sqrt{2}$, and bias within superconducting gap $|eV| < \Delta$. Holds under weak bond and onsite disorder.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Topological protection of perfect CAR. (a) Map of $\eta$ versus $\epsilon_{0}$ and $t^{\prime}$ at zero bias. The phase winding of the electron reflection (ER) amplitude along the indicated closed loop yields $W=1$ , topologically guaranteeing a zero of ER (perfect CAR) within the enclosed region. (b) Trajectory of the perfect CAR condition in the $(E,\epsilon_{0},t^{\prime})$ parameter space. Other parameters are the same as in Fig. 2 .
fields.figure_gloss: Logarithmic nonlocal conductance $\eta$ mapped against interface energy $\epsilon_{0}$ and junction hopping $t'/t$. The closed loop yields a topological phase winding number $W=1$, protecting a zero-reflection node (unit CAR).

fields.result: Per-run encoder reseeding reduces mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 under a seed-aware fault selection to 0.020 under a seed-blind fault selection at width $n=8$ and depth $d=12$. Rejection causes the 86.7% reduction.
fields.question: How much per-run encoder reseeding reduces accepted logical corruption under different attacker-knowledge models.
fields.prior: Fixed distance-three $[[5,1,3]]$ code corrects 100% of tested weight-one Pauli faults, whereas only 18.5% of sampled random Clifford encoders satisfy exact correction.
fields.limits: Restricted to Clifford encoders up to $n=17$, weight-one local Pauli injections, and gate-local depolarizing noise rates of $p_{1}=10^{-3}$ and $p_{2}=10^{-2}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: HSE ablation and attacker knowledge. Left: paired ablation at $(n,k,d)=(8,1,12)$ over 200 seeds. (a) Change in worst-fault disturbance relative to the full HSE; squares show means and shading the central 90%. (b) Fraction of seeds safe against every tested fault; labels give mean two-qubit instruction counts. Right: (c) held-out scores at $n=8$ for seed-aware, seed-blind, and uniformly random fault selection. Bars show 95% intervals.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots disturbance relative to full HSE and safe seed fraction (left panels) and held-out scores at $n=8$ (right panel). Demonstrates that seed-blind performance approaches random fault selection while seed-aware attackers cause higher disturbance.

fields.result: CHSH violation without recovery operations is impossible for particle survival probability $\eta\le 1/2$. Explicit permutation-invariant Dicke encodings achieve recovery-free CHSH violation for $\eta > (\sqrt{5}-1)/2$.
fields.question: Can CHSH nonlocality survive particle loss without applying an explicit recovery operation?
fields.limits: Asymptotically large particle number $n\to\infty$ and excitation limit $N\to\infty$. Evaluated under unflagged deletion and flagged erasure noise models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Recovery-free CHSH violation under particle loss for the PI protocols. The dashed horizontal line is the local bound $S=2$ . For the one-excitation encoding ( $N=1$ ), the threshold is $\eta=1/\sqrt{2}$ . For the large- $n$ limit, increasing $N$ lowers the onset of CHSH violation toward $\eta_{G}=(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$ , the threshold obtained by optimizing over finite $N$ . We find no protocol such that $S>2$ for $1/2\leq\eta\leq\eta_{G}$ (Supp. Mat. S4.4).
fields.figure_gloss: Plots the CHSH parameter $S$ against survival probability $\eta$ for various excitation numbers $N$. It shows the violation threshold $S>2$ moving from $\eta=1/\sqrt{2}$ at $N=1$ toward $\eta_G=(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$ as $N$ increases.

fields.result: Analytical characterization of Gaussian quantum networks achieving perfect local privacy while reaching Heisenberg scaling in sensitivity with photon number and sensing mode count.
fields.question: How to construct optimal Gaussian networks for private distributed quantum sensing under perfect local privacy constraints.
fields.limits: Applies to phase estimation with Gaussian probe states under arbitrary phase-independent quantum channels.

fields.result:
Zero-temperature linear conductance for unhybridized MBSs ($
u_M=0$) is non-zero only at magnetic flux phase $
u=(2n+1)
u$ ($n\in\mathbb{Z}$) and scales as $\mathcal{G}=2q\alpha e^2/[h(\alpha+1)]$. For hybridized MBSs ($
u_M\neq 0$), conductance oscillation period shifts from $2\nu$ to $4\nu$ when quantum dot energy level $\varepsilon_d\neq\varepsilon_F$.
fields.question: How do leads-QD coupling asymmetry $\alpha$ and bias voltage asymmetry $q$ modify the linear conductance signatures of Majorana bound states in quantum dot-nanowire junctions?
fields.prior: Generalizes the symmetric coupling case ($\alpha=1$, $q=0.5$) where zero-temperature, zero-bias conductance is $e^2/(2h)$ (Liu and Baranger).
fields.limits: Theoretical calculation in the low-energy transport regime. Assumes noninteracting single-level QD and Zeeman energy $E_Z>\sqrt{\Delta^2+\mu_w^2}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: The linear conductance $\mathcal{G}$ in the case of unhybridized MBSs ( $\varepsilon_{M}/\Gamma=0$ ) as a function of magnetic flux phase $\phi$ and bias voltage asymmetry parameter $q$ for different values of the leads–QD coupling asymmetry parameter $\alpha$ : (a) and (d) $\alpha=0.5$ , (b) and (e) $\alpha=1$ and (c) and (f) $\alpha=5$ . The temperature is fixed at $k_{B}T/\Gamma=0.3$ and the QD–MBSs coupling strengths are $|\lambda_{1}|/\Gamma=0.3$ and $|\lambda_{2}|/\Gamma=0.1$ , respectively. The QD characteristic energy is (a)–(c) $\varepsilon_{d}/\Gamma=0$ and (d)–(f) $\varepsilon_{d}/\Gamma=-1$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Linear conductance $\mathcal{G}$ mapped against magnetic flux phase $\phi$ (horizontal axis) and bias asymmetry $q$ (vertical axis) for different leads-QD coupling ratios $\alpha$. Shows conductance peak locations shifting from $\phi=2n\pi$ to $\phi=(2n+1)\pi$ as $q$ increases.

fields.result: In a gapless normal wire, even- and odd-parity capacitance resonances are separated by $35.0\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ in dot potential, while in a topological wire they are separated by only $5.25\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ and persist over a gate-voltage window of $-50\,\mu\mathrm{eV}\leq\delta\mu\leq 50\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$.
fields.question: Can quantum capacitance signatures of topological Majorana zero modes be experimentally distinguished from those of a non-superconducting gapless wire segment?
fields.limits: Clean wire benchmark and correlated-disorder model with finite Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Low-energy limit involving two or three single-particle levels.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Flux-maximized parity-resolved capacitance in the clean systems. Maximum of $|C_{\mathrm{Q}}|$ over $\phi$ as a function of $\delta V_{\mathrm{QD}}$ for the gapless (left) and topological (right) wires. Solid blue and dashed red curves denote even and odd parity, respectively. The gapless maxima lie near the separate $\tau$ and $g$ resonances and are separated by $35.00\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ , whereas the topological maxima remain within the same gate region and are separated by $5.25\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ . Colored vertical lines mark the maxima, the black dash-dotted line marks $\delta V_{\mathrm{QD}}=0$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Plots the maximum quantum capacitance over magnetic flux against dot potential detuning for gapless (left) and topological (right) wires. Gapless system shows two distinct, separated parity resonances, whereas topological system shows overlapping parity branches within a single broader gate window.

fields.result: Steady-state current factorizes into reciprocal spectral current and phase-asymmetric occupation imbalance $I_{\rm ss}=I_{A}P_{\gamma}$, producing diode response without Andreev spectrum asymmetry.
fields.question: Can a Josephson junction with a reciprocal Andreev channel acquire a diode response through nonequilibrium occupation?
fields.limits: Infinite-gap limit, large loss rate $\kappa \gg t,\Gamma$, and secular limit $\Gamma_{\pm} \ll 2E_{A}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure S3: Finite- $\kappa$ diode efficiency from the direct Lindblad solution at $t=\Gamma_{L}=\Gamma_{R}=1$ and zero onsite energies, $\epsilon_{L}=\epsilon_{R}=0$ . (a) Diode efficiency $\eta_{D}$ in the $(\chi,\kappa)$ plane. The broad region with $\eta_{D}\simeq 1$ shows that the backward-current branch is strongly suppressed relative to the forward branch. (b) $\eta_{D}$ versus reservoir phase $\chi$ for $\kappa=1,3,10$ , together with the analytic Zeno result of Eq. ( S64 ) ( $\kappa\to\infty$ , dashed). Reversing $\chi$ reverses the diode polarity, $\eta_{D}(-\chi)=-\eta_{D}(\chi)$ . (c) $\eta_{D}$ versus $\kappa$ at fixed $\chi=0.1\pi$ and $0.3\pi$ . Dashed lines denote the corresponding $\kappa\to\infty$ values.
fields.figure_gloss: Diode efficiency $\eta_D$ plotted against reservoir phase $\chi$ and dissipation rate $\kappa$. Shows saturation to ideal efficiency $\eta_D \simeq 1$ and convergence to the analytical Zeno limit as $\kappa$ increases.

fields.result: Neural-augmented bidirectional message-passing decoding raises the depolarizing pseudo-threshold of the concatenated $[[15,7,3]]$ quantum Hamming code to $12.3\%$.
fields.question: Can high-rate concatenated quantum codes be decoded accurately and generically with bounded worst-case latency?
fields.prior: Was $6.5\%$ using a bidirectional hard-decision decoder.
fields.limits: Evaluated in numerical simulations under phenomenological and circuit-level depolarizing noise models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Block failure rate of the concatenated $[[15,7,3]]$ Hamming code at concatenation depths $L=2$ and $L=3$ , comparing the neural message-passing (MP) decoder with the bidirectional hard-decision decoder. (a) Under bit-flip noise, the neural MP decoder raises the pseudo-threshold from $p^{\ast}\approx 4.4\%$ to $6.8\%$ . (b) Under depolarizing noise, it nearly doubles the pseudo-threshold, from $p^{\ast}\approx 6.5\%$ to $12.3\%$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Block failure rate plotted against physical error probability for concatenation depths $L=2$ and $L=3$. Compares the neural message-passing decoder with the bidirectional hard-decision decoder under bit-flip and depolarizing noise.

fields.result: L-NBP attains an error threshold of $17.5\%$ under depolarizing code-capacity noise with linear $\mathcal{O}(n)$ complexity, while matching BP-OSD accuracy at distance $d=9$ under circuit-level noise using $0.2\%$ of its FLOPs.
fields.question: Can belief propagation decoding on surface codes achieve high logical accuracy and clear threshold behavior while preserving linear complexity?
fields.prior: BP-OSD achieved a threshold of $16.5\%$ at $1.95$ M FLOPs ($d=13$), AMBP achieved $17.0\%$ at $95$ M FLOPs, and QECCT achieved $17.1\%$ at $604$ M FLOPs under code-capacity noise.
fields.limits: Evaluated via numerical simulations on rotated surface codes up to distance $d=13$ under code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise models.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus physical error rate across code distances under code-capacity noise, showing the $17.5\%$ threshold for L-NBP, and a comparison of FLOPs versus threshold at $d=13$ across decoders.

fields.result: DPU-based near-memory processing achieves $1.071\times 10^{7}$ decodes/s for normalized Min-Sum BP on the $[[144,12,12]]$ code at $p=0.001$ with 1 iteration, while keeping serialized $X+Z$ compute latency to $0.873\text{ ms}$ at 5 iterations.
fields.question: Can processing-in-memory architectures provide high throughput and sub-millisecond compute latency for iterative belief-propagation decoding of quantum LDPC codes?
fields.prior: 16-logical-CPU baseline achieved $1.22\times 10^{6}$ decodes/s under the same conditions ($8.8\times$ lower).
fields.limits: Simulated kernel execution via uPIMulator under data-qubit Pauli error model with ideal syndrome measurements; excludes host-DPU communication latency.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Decoding throughput of the 16-logical-CPU baseline and the 2,560-DPU configuration at $p=0.001$ as the number of BP iterations increases. The DPU throughput is derived from per-DPU uPIMulator cycle counts under the concurrent independent-DPU execution model. The inset enlarges the throughput comparison for eight to ten BP iterations.
fields.figure_gloss: Projected decoding throughput versus BP iterations for the 2,560-DPU configuration compared to the 16-logical-CPU baseline at $p=0.001$.

fields.result: Theoretical prepare-and-measure DSQC protocol combines classical Reed-Solomon erasure coding with transverse spatial qudits, yielding intercept-resend error rate $E_{IR} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d-1}{d}$ across $b=2$ mutually unbiased bases without quantum memory or entanglement.
fields.question: Can high-dimensional qudits and classical erasure coding implement deterministic secure quantum communication resilient to noise without requiring quantum memory?
fields.limits: Theoretical design; assumes single-photon heralded states, prime alphabet dimension $q$, and total photons per block $n < q$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Proposed experimental setup using photon pairs from SPDC to produce heralded single photons. See more details in the main text.
fields.figure_gloss: Proposed experimental setup for high-dimensional DSQC using SPDC heralded photon pairs, spatial modulation via SLM or DMD, and time-gated matrix single-photon detection.

fields.result: Quasi-local renormalization-group decoder initialized with target and buffer sizes $a_0=b_0=d/8$ achieves a whole-system logical-failure crossing window at physical error rate $p_{\times}^{\mathrm{comp}} \approx 0.09\text{--}0.10$.
fields.question: How much of the global minimum-weight perfect matching correction inside a target region is determined by syndrome data in a finite surrounding buffer?
fields.prior: Conventional global minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) threshold for the dephased toric code is $p_c^{\mathrm{MWPM}} \approx 0.103$ (Dennis et al. 2002; Wang et al. 2003).
fields.limits: Restricted to dephasing noise (pure $Z$ errors) with perfect syndrome measurements on the 2D periodic toric code. Patch sizes scale as $O(d)$ rather than constant depth.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Logical-failure data for the composite quasi-local decoder. For each syndrome sample, the decoder runs local MWPM on active patches, commits only corrections inside each target region $A$ , updates the residual syndrome, and, if residual defects remain, merges to the next RG round according to Eq. ( 10 ) and repeats. The dataset shown here uses the tuned initialization $a_{0}=b_{0}=d/8$ . Panel (a) shows the resulting logical-failure curves versus $p$ , with an apparent crossing window $p_{\times}^{\mathrm{comp}}\approx 0.09$ – $0.10$ . Panel (b) shows the finite-size collapse of the same data.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical failure probability versus physical error rate $p$ for code distances $d$ using the composite quasi-local RG decoder with $a_0=b_0=d/8$, exhibiting a crossing near $p \approx 0.09\text{--}0.10$ along with its finite-size scaling collapse.

fields.result: Dual-isotope (${}^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$-g, ${}^{174}\mathrm{Yb}$) surface code with in-place readout achieves lowest logical error rate, where Rydberg-state decay accounts for 74% to 80% of the logical error rate scaling.
fields.question: How do realistic systemic noise channels affect the surface-code quantum memory performance of dual-isotope ytterbium arrays compared to single-isotope architectures?
fields.limits: Simulations using Clifford-compatible twirled noise models; atom-loss detection flags not decoded; specific experimental noise parameters assumed.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5 : The dependence of the LER per round of the rotated and XZZX surface codes at code distance $d$ for different configurations of isotope, encoding and SE measurement method. Colour and marker delineate the isotope combination and encoding, and the line style represents the SE method. The dual-isotope configuration using normal SE with in-place measurement (blue solid line with circle marker) achieves the lowest LER among all the configurations. The SWAP SE cases (dashed line) achieve similar or higher LER compared to normal SE for all configurations on the rotated surface code. Moreover, comparing the two codes, the XZZX code achieves a LER comparable to or lower than that of the rotated surface code.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate per round versus code distance $d$ across various isotope pairings, qubit encodings, and syndrome extraction schemes for rotated and XZZX surface codes.

fields.result: Asymmetric qubitization outperforms Trotterization and qDRIFT in T-gate scaling for SYK simulation, requiring under $5\times 10^8$ T gates for $N=100$ Majorana modes at total error $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}=10^{-4}$ (versus $>4\times 10^9$ for qDRIFT), despite needing 159 qubits instead of 50.
fields.question: What are the concrete qubit and T-gate resource requirements for simulating the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model across Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization algorithms?
fields.limits: Theoretical worst-case upper bounds used for PPR method resource scaling; assumed evolution time $t=1$ and split error equally between algorithm and rotation synthesis ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rot}}$).
tools: Asymmetric qubitization with Quantum Signal Processing
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3: Qubit counts and total T gates as a function of the number of Majorana modes. The top plot shows the scaling in qubit count, while the bottom plot gives the scaling for the total number of T gates required. PPR based methods provide a better qubit count, but their T count (with qDRIFT requiring fewer resources) is much higher than the one for AQ. For the T gate scaling $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}$ is fixed at $10^{-4}$ . Coupling constants were again fixed equivalently for all methods ( $Jt=24$ for Trotter and qDRIFT and $Jt=1$ for AQ).
fields.figure_gloss: Qubit count (top) and total T gates at $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}=10^{-4}$ (bottom) versus number of Majorana modes $N$ for Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization at $t=1$. Asymmetric qubitization requires more qubits (159 vs 50 at $N=100$) but yields orders of magnitude fewer T gates.

fields.result: Explicit quantum Fourier transform circuits scale as $\operatorname{poly}(\log q, \log(1/\varepsilon))$ gates for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and remove the $|F| = \operatorname{poly}(n)$ size restriction for wreath products $F \wr S_n$.
fields.question: How can efficient non-abelian quantum Fourier transform circuits be systematically constructed for broader classes of finite groups, including finite linear groups and general wreath products?
fields.prior: For finite Lie-type groups of rank $k$, cost was $q^{O(k)}$ operations (Moore, Rockmore, and Russell); for wreath products $H \wr S_n$, prior generic constructions required $|H| = \operatorname{poly}(n)$.
fields.limits: Operator-norm precision $\varepsilon$, with gate counts scaling polylogarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$.

fields.result: Incorporating pairwise classical feature dependencies into quantum feature maps via controlled-$R_Y(\theta)$ gates affects QSVM binary classification, but simpler encodings (Angle-RY and Z feature Map) often achieve the top composite Quantum Feature Encoding Score by reducing circuit cost and generalization gap.
fields.question: How does incorporating statistical dependency structures of classical data into quantum feature maps affect QSVM classification performance and circuit complexity compared to predefined conventional quantum feature maps?
fields.limits: Evaluated via state vector simulation on five binary classification datasets, using PCA reduction (14 components) for high-dimensional data, without physical hardware noise.
tools: Pearson, Spearman, Kendall Tau, Mutual Information, Distance Correlation
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Comparison of training and test accuracy across encoding strategies for the EEG Eye State Classification Dataset.
fields.figure_gloss: Training and test classification accuracy across 11 encoding strategies for the EEG Eye State classification dataset.

fields.result: Spectral coordinate embedding for Quantum DeepONet trunk networks reduces mean relative $L^{2}$ error across four PDE benchmarks by $36.0\%$ to $54.1\%$. Qubit count and circuit depth remain completely unchanged.
fields.question: Can coordinate-matched classical spectral embeddings eliminate spectral bias in Quantum DeepONet trunk networks without increasing quantum resource costs?
fields.prior: Baseline Quantum DeepONet mean relative $L^{2}$ error was $1.159\%$ (antiderivative), $3.463\%$ (advection), $2.313\%$ (Burgers), and $5.889\%$ (channel Poisson).
fields.limits: Ideal, noiseless, infinite-shot quantum simulation only; single training seed per arm; tested exclusively on smooth or strongly smoothed PDE solutions.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Advection: mean relative $L^{2}$ error over $200$ test functions, with standard-deviation bars. Quantum SEDONet improves on the baseline for $199$ of $200$ functions (paired $t=23.3$ ).
fields.figure_gloss: Mean relative $L^{2}$ test error for the advection benchmark. Shows Quantum SEDONet cutting baseline Quantum DeepONet error from $3.463\%$ to $1.744\%$ across 200 test samples.

fields.result: A uniform Zeeman field $M_z$ modulates and can completely reverse single-electron charge polarization $P_L - P_R$ in an asymmetric double quantum dot without altering electrostatic detuning.
fields.question: Can a spatially uniform magnetic Zeeman field control left-right charge polarization in an open double quantum dot?
fields.limits: Interaction-dominated regime where interdot tunneling $t_{12}$ and lead coupling $\gamma$ are smaller than Coulomb interactions $U_i, U_{12}$; wide-band limit for electronic reservoirs.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Magnetic charge reconfiguration for $U_{1}=U_{2}$ . (a,b) Maximum field-induced changes $\Delta P_{L,R}^{\max}(v_{1},v_{2})=\max_{|M_{z}|\leq 1}|P_{L,R}(v_{1},v_{2};M_{z})-P_{L,R}(v_{1},v_{2};0)|$ , restricted to $P_{N=1}\geq 0.95$ throughout the field sweep $|M_{z}|\leq 1$ . (c) Left, right, and total single-electron probabilities and (d) the four spin-resolved single-electron probabilities versus $M_{z}$ at $v_{1}=-1.5$ and $v_{2}=-2$ . Parameters are $U_{1}=U_{2}=4$ , $U_{12}=3$ , $t_{12}=0.3$ , $T=0.05$ , and $\gamma=0.05$ , with $\Delta_{i\sigma}=-i\gamma/2$ . The red dashed line in (a,b) denotes the boundary $P_{N=1}=0.95$ and the white regions outside the red dashed line do not satisfy the $P_{N=1}\geq 0.95$ criterion.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots maximum change in dot occupation probabilities $\Delta P_{L,R}^{\max}$ across bare gate levels $(v_1, v_2)$ under a swept Zeeman field $|M_z| \leq 1$, showing substantial charge transfer while maintaining $P_{N=1} \simeq 1$.

fields.result: AFM-based local Stark gating resolves and localizes individual interlayer excitonic quantum emitters separated by $d_{D3-D4}=(39\pm 19)$ nm and $d_{D1-D2}=(41\pm 15)$ nm, with single-emitter localization resolution limit $\Delta y_{D1}\simeq 20$ nm.
fields.question: Can subwavelength-confined 2D quantum emitters be spatially resolved and individually controlled in energy, charge state, and radiative lifetime beyond the optical diffraction limit?
fields.limits: Base temperature 4 K in cryostat; top and bottom hBN flake thicknesses between 15 nm and 20 nm; emitter position extraction relies on uniform in-plane dipole offset across single domain.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Super-resolution localization of 2D quantum emitters. a, Tip-position dependence of the PL emission spectrum from spot B of device 1. The spectra are collected sequentially while the tip is raster scanned on a $400$ nm square, with $5$ nm step size and $V_{\text{tip}}=-1$ V. White lines separate the tip line scans along the $y$ direction (fast axis) at a fixed $x$ coordinate (slow axis). The panel displays only the central region of the raster scan, i.e. $225$ nm of the slow axis rangex. b, Tip-position-dependent energy shift of the dot at around $1,366$ meV extracted from panel a . The backlash of the fast $y$ axis is corrected by shifting 3 pixels. c, Line-cut (blue circles) of b taken along the $x$ direction, averaged from $y=200$ to $220$ nm. The red curve is calculated from equation 1 with a global scaling factor $A=0.22$ , and electron-hole displacement ${\bf d}=(3.5,\penalty\ 0,\penalty\ 0.7)$ nm, while the electric field at the dot position is simulated as described in the Methods. d, Representative tip line-scan along the $y$ direction at $V_{\text{tip}}=-1$ , at Spot C of device 1. e, Line cuts at fixed PL energies corresponding to the black arrows in d . The FWHM of the most red-shifted peak is marked in red, and measure approximately $20$ nm. f, Extracted positions of seven emitters in a squared area of $250$ nm in Spot C. The error bars corresponds to the FWHM of the most red-shifted peak, as in the example of panel e .
fields.figure_gloss: PL emission and Stark shifts under AFM tip raster scanning. Extracted sub-diffraction spatial map of 7 individual localized emitters in a $250\text{ nm}\times 250\text{ nm}$ area with emitter separations down to roughly 40 nm.

fields.result: Microscopic theory with continuous exciton momenta reproduces multidimensional coherent spectroscopy peak hierarchies, broadening, and cross-peak interference in monolayer $\mathrm{MoSe}_2$ via phase-space filling polaron interactions.
fields.question: How do continuous momentum degrees of freedom and microscopic many-body interactions shape multidimensional coherent spectroscopy spectra of excitons and exciton-polarons in 2D semiconductors?
fields.prior: Calculated attractive-polaron-attractive-polaron interaction strengths differ by less than 16% at $E_{\rm F}/\varepsilon_{\rm T}=1$ and under 10% for $E_{\rm F}/\varepsilon_{\rm T}\lesssim 0.4$ compared to the Chevy ansatz in Ref. [31] (Sidler et al., 2017).
fields.limits: Dipole approximation for light-matter coupling; pure ground state; identical co-circular excitons; electron-electron and exciton-exciton exchange processes neglected.
tools: Chevy ansatz / truncation of the basis
fields.figure_caption: Figure 11: Strengths of interactions between two attractive polarons (blue), between an attractive and a repulsive polaron (orange), and between two repulsive polarons (green). Solid lines are differences in eigenenergies between Eqs. ( 51 ) and ( 47 ), while dashed lines are calculated from eigenstates of Eqs. ( 47 ) alone using Eq. ( 52 ). The vertical dashed line indicates the doping level used in Figs. 8 and 9 .
fields.figure_gloss: Interaction energy shifts per area as a function of Fermi energy $E_{\rm F}/\varepsilon_{\rm T}$ for attractive-attractive, attractive-repulsive, and repulsive-repulsive polaron pairs, showing transition from attractive to repulsive polaron-polaron interactions at higher doping.

fields.result: Crystal-phase quantum dots in AlGaAs nanowire cores achieve narrow exciton and biexciton linewidths of 104 µeV and 61 µeV (${\pm 4}$ µeV) with 1 ns exciton lifetime indicating type-I band alignment.
fields.question: Can crystal-phase quantum dots in AlGaAs nanowires overcome the broad emission linewidths and type-II band alignment typical of binary crystal-phase quantum dots?
fields.prior: Crystal-phase quantum dots in binary semiconductors such as InP and GaAs typically exhibit emission linewidths in the meV range and exciton lifetimes of tens of nanoseconds.
fields.limits: Nanowire core diameter 7 to 20 nm; zincblende insertion density 15 to 50 insertions/µm; timing resolution of correlation measurements limited by detector jitter (FWHM $\gtrsim 505$ ps or 110 ps).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Exciton - biexciton complex in an AlGaAs CPQD. (a) Power-dependent micro-photoluminescence showing exciton (X) and biexciton (XX) states. Only emission with vertical polarization is acquired (see Figure 4 for horizontal polarization). (b) Time-resolved photoluminescence of the exciton line. The decay is fitted (red) with the sum of two decaying exponentials, which are also plotted separately in dashed lines. The extracted characteristic times are plotted next to each decay. (c) Cross-correlation between the exciton and biexciton emission lines showing a strong bunching consistent with cascade emission. For positive delay, the start channel is the biexciton emission and the stop channel is the exciton emission; the opposite order holds for negative delay. (d) Autocorrelation measurement of the exciton line showing antibunching. The data are fitted with a two-exponential $g^{(2)}(\tau)$ function accounting for antibunching (characteristic time $\tau_{a}$ ) and power bunching (characteristic time $\tau_{b}$ ). The transparent grey line is the fit to the data, and the red line corresponds to the same fit partially corrected for the non-ideal instrument response function (they are very close to each other). See Sections 3 and 4 for details of the fit.
fields.figure_gloss: Excitation power dependence, decay kinetics, and photon correlation histograms showing clean exciton-biexciton emission, 1 ns radiative lifetime, and antibunching from an AlGaAs crystal-phase quantum dot.

fields.result: Introduces $\varepsilon$-stable representations $\rho\otimes\varepsilon\simeq\rho$ for 1D irreducible representations $\varepsilon$ of order $d$, proving they yield protected $d$-dimensional logical qudit subspaces with cyclic shift $X_L$ implemented by ribbon operators. Realizes logical qubits in $S_n$ ($n\ge 3$), a logical qutrit with universal gates in $A_4$, and qudits for any $d\ge 2$ via $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^d\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_d$.
fields.question: What general group-theoretic conditions allow finite-group Kitaev quantum double models to support protected logical qudits?
fields.limits: Universal computation construction assumes existence of deterministic quasiparticle transport operators $M_\xi^\rho$.

fields.result: Derives message-passing decoders from parent classical LDPC decoders to resolve stabilizer-induced trapping sets directly, decoding lifted-product codes on a phenomenological graph without auxiliary CNOT variable nodes or OSD post-processing.
fields.question: How can QLDPC decoders achieve fast, fault-tolerant decoding under circuit-level noise without OSD post-processing and auxiliary CNOT correlation nodes?
fields.prior: BP+OSD (BP_OSD) required cubic-complexity linear-system solves over large Tanner graphs expanded with auxiliary correlation nodes for CNOT faults.
fields.limits: Evaluated on lifted-product (LP) codes under circuit-level noise through simulations.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 2 : Node types in the Tanner graphs of HGP/LP codes. VV-type variable nodes are depicted with a circle inside another circle because they are obtained by multiplying two variable nodes, each represented by a single circle. Analogously, CC-type variable nodes, $X$ -checks, and $Z$ -checks are represented, respectively, by a square inside another square, a circle inside a square, and a square inside a circle.
fields.figure_gloss: Classification of product nodes in the base graph of HGP and LP codes, showing VV-type and CC-type variable nodes alongside X-check and Z-check nodes.

fields.result: Surveys the physics, current status, and scaling bottlenecks of neutral atom quantum processors across alkali ($^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$, $^{133}\mathrm{Cs}$) and alkaline-earth-like ($^{88}\mathrm{Sr}$, $\mathrm{Yb}$) architectures.
fields.question: What is the physical and architectural status of neutral atom systems for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing?
fields.limits: Circuits currently limited to a few hundred operations due to recoil heating, atom loss, SLM pixel bounds ($<10^5$ sites), and optical power dissipation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Demonstrations of large qubit arrays. 87 Rb: Nearly defect free square array with 2024 atoms in 2025 sites ( Lin et al. (2025) ); 133 Cs: averaged image of atoms in a 12,001 site array ( Manetsch et al. (2025) ); 88 Sr: more than 1000 atoms loaded into an optical lattice ( Gyger et al. (2024) ); 171 Yb: 1225 site array with 99% filling fraction loaded from a reservoir ( Norcia et al. (2024) ).
fields.figure_gloss: Images and arrangements of large neutral atom arrays across different atomic species, showing arrays scaling from 1,000 to over 12,000 sites.

fields.result: Formulates quantum block turbo codes using product structures of constituent stabilizer codes. Fifth iteration of $\left[\!\left[64,9,9\right]\!\right]$ QBTC achieves estimated word error rate of $6\times 10^{-7}$ at $10^{-2}$ depolarizing rate.
fields.question: How to adapt classical block turbo codes and iterative product-code decoding to quantum error correction.
fields.limits: Depolarizing channel simulation. Requires classical soft-information processing for component decoders.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 6: Comparison performances of QBTC $\left[\!\left[5,1,3\right]\!\right]\times\left[\!\left[5,1,3\right]\!\right]$ , QBTC $\left[\!\left[8,3,3\right]\!\right]\times\left[\!\left[8,3,3\right]\!\right]$ (linear extrapolation at $10^{-2}$ ) and Poulin’s message passing (MP) decoding [ 23 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Plots word error rate against channel depolarizing rate. Shows turbo decoding iterations improving error rates for $\left[\!\left[8,3,3\right]\!\right]\times\left[\!\left[8,3,3\right]\!\right]$ code compared to single-qubit product code and message-passing baselines.

fields.result: Bosonic codes on hyperbolic Riemann surfaces ($g \geq 2$) have stabilizer groups $\pi_1(\Sigma_g)$ that are non-amenable, forcing a strictly positive spectral gap in $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{stab}}$ that precludes normalizable states satisfying all stabilizer conditions.
fields.question: What bosonic quantum error-correcting codes emerge when phase space is a compact Riemann surface of genus $g \geq 2$?
fields.limits: Holds for compact Riemann surfaces with genus $g \geq 2$. Non-amenability prevents normalizable code states even approximately.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: (a) Single-generator conditional-kick protocol ( $k=2$ , Bolza surface, $N_{\mathrm{trunc}}=60$ , $\varepsilon=0.5$ ): population in the $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{\gamma}$ -eigenbasis at rounds $t=0,20,100,400$ . The dashed line marks $\varphi=0$ (target stabilizer phase); population concentrates there over successive rounds. (b) Circuit-QED module: two microwave cavities ( $\hat{a}$ , $\hat{b}$ ) dispersively coupled ( $\chi$ ) to a transmon ancilla, with a single parametric pump ( $\Lambda$ ) driving correlated photon-pair creation (two-mode squeezing). The effective Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\chi\,\hat{n}_{c}(\hat{n}_{a}+\hat{n}_{b})+\Lambda\,\hat{K}_{\phi}$ provides the native gate set. (c) One round of the conditional-kick channel: controlled $\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{\gamma}=e^{i\theta\hat{K}_{\phi}}$ (parametric squeeze) followed by a classically conditioned correction $\hat{V}_{\varepsilon}=e^{i\varepsilon\hat{K}_{z}}$ (cross-Kerr), repeated for each generator $\gamma\in\Gamma$ . (d) Stabilizer energy $\langle\hat{H}_{\mathrm{stab}}\rangle(t)$ [Eq. ( 13 )] for $s=1,2,3,4$ generators ( $N_{\mathrm{trunc}}=200$ ). The single-generator (amenable) protocol drives $\langle\hat{H}_{\mathrm{stab}}\rangle$ toward zero, while all multi-generator (non-amenable) protocols collapse onto a common $\mathcal{O}(1)$ plateau set by the spectral gap (Theorem 1 ). The floor is independent of $N_{\mathrm{trunc}}$ (not shown).
fields.figure_gloss: Panel (d) shows the average stabilizer energy $\langle\hat{H}_{\mathrm{stab}}\rangle(t)$ versus protocol rounds $t$. A single generator ($s=1$, amenable) drives energy toward zero, while multiple non-commuting generators ($s=2,3,4$, non-amenable) hit a non-zero $\mathcal{O}(1)$ plateau dictated by the spectral gap.

fields.result: A single recovery map simultaneously corrects every $\mathcal{E}$-controlled channel with worst-case error bounded by environment-leakage distance and average-case error bounded by Knill--Laflamme Hellinger distance. For fixed code and error set, the average-case optimal error of channel-dependent recovery is achieved by a single universal recovery map.
fields.question: Whether uniform protection against $\mathcal{E}$-controlled channels in approximate quantum error correction extends to a universal decoding operation independent of the specific noise channel.
fields.prior: Uniform approximate guarantees were proved separately for each channel in arXiv:2607.22995, requiring channel-dependent recovery maps.
fields.limits: Finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; channels must have Kraus expansions in $\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{E})$ with coefficient matrix norm bounded by 1.

fields.result: Presents dataset across 31 Dicke target states $D_N^K$ ($N=5$ to $14$, depth $m=0$ to $200$ sub-rounds) and hardware benchmarks on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald processor, where measured circuits retain up to $0.758$ of noiseless fidelity.
fields.question: How do state-preparation fidelity, circuit depth, and hardware gate overhead trade off when generating multipartite Dicke states via collision models?
fields.limits: Circuit depth capped at $m=200$ sub-rounds; noiseless L1 yields lower bounds rather than certified global optima; 544 of 6,231 cost rows are upper bounds; hardware results reflect a single session on 10 arms without physical excitation-number heralding.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Estimated unconditional fidelity $F$ for each measured hardware arm. The horizontal dash above each bar indicates the noiseless fidelity $F_{\rm ideal}$ of the corresponding circuit, and the native two-qubit gate count is shown beneath each bar. Error bars show the quoted uncertainty $\sigma_{F}$ obtained from the error-bar analysis described in Sec. IV.3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Unconditional state fidelity $F$ across hardware measurement arms on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor compared to the ideal noiseless fidelity $F_{\rm ideal}$ and native two-qubit gate count.

fields.result: Analytic robust self-testing bound for $n$-qubit GHZ states certifies extractability $\Xi\geq s_n\beta+\mu$ (with $s_n=(\sqrt{2}+1)/2^{n/2}$ and $\mu=-(1+\sqrt{2})$) under MABK inequality violation $\beta$, maintaining constant noise tolerance independent of party number $n$.
fields.question: How does the robust self-testing bound for multipartite GHZ states scale with the number of parties $n$ under Bell inequality violations?
fields.prior: Existing analytic bounds for general $n$ tolerated violation errors that shrank polynomially (McKague et al.) or exponentially (Sarkar et al.) with $n$, failing to give nontrivial certification beyond $n\ge 10$ even at $10^{-5}$ relative violation deficiency.
fields.limits: Analytic bound is within a constant factor of 2 in slope from the theoretical upper bound; the exact optimal bound is verified numerically via polynomial-size grid search up to $n=100$.
tools: simplex grid search and gradient descent
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Tolerance versus number of parties: largest relative violation deficiency $\eta=\varepsilon/\beta_{nQ}$ certifying $\Xi\geq 1/2$ . The proved bound and the upper bound of Eq. ( 3 ) are flat in $n$ (a constant factor-of-two gap), whereas the previously known analytic tests for all $n$ (McKague) decay with the number of parties; the shaded band at $n\leq 7$ marks the reach of numerical operator-inequality bounds.
fields.figure_gloss: Tolerable relative violation deficiency $\eta=\varepsilon/\beta_{nQ}$ for extractability $\Xi\ge 1/2$ plotted against party number $n$. Proved and theoretical upper bounds remain constant across all $n$, whereas prior analytic bounds decay rapidly toward zero.

fields.result: Non-Markovian open quantum dynamics for heavy-ion probes can be simulated via an auxiliary two-level pseudomode qubit coupled to a memoryless bath, which requires one extra persistent qubit and smoothly converges to the Markovian limit as $\tau_c \to 0$.
fields.question: How can open-quantum-system dynamics beyond the Markovian limit be simulated efficiently on a quantum computer for hard probes in heavy-ion collisions?
fields.limits: Two-level bound-state subsystem, static and homogeneous thermal medium, exponentially decaying medium correlation function, weak subsystem-bath coupling.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Survival probability $P_{\rm bound}(t)$ of the bound state as a function of time at $\Delta E\equiv E_{b}=0.3$ GeV, $T=0.5$ GeV, and $\lambda_{\rm pm}^{2}=0.5$ GeV. The dashed curve shows the Markovian solution [i.e., Eq. ( 50 )], while the square, triangle, and open-circle markers display the non-Markovian [i.e., Eq. ( 46 )] quantum-circuit-based computations with $\tau_{c}=10.0$ , $5.0$ , and $0.5$ GeV -1 , respectively. As $\tau_{c}$ decreases, the non-Markovian curves converge onto the Markovian reference calculated with $\tau_{c}=0.1~{\rm GeV}^{-1}$ . The simulation parameters are $\Delta t=0.01$ GeV -1 , $N_{\rm step}=10000$ , resulting in a total simulated time of $100$ GeV -1 .
fields.figure_gloss: Bound-state survival probability $P_{\rm bound}(t)$ plotted versus time $t$ for non-Markovian quantum-circuit simulations at memory times $\tau_c = 10.0, 5.0, 0.5\text{ GeV}^{-1}$ compared to the Markovian solution at $\tau_c = 0.1\text{ GeV}^{-1}$.

fields.result: Deploy-quantum models trained by classically matching low-order moments or $\mathrm{MMD}^2$ fail to generalize: IQP Born machine coverage decouples from loss and remains near the random baseline $C_{\mathrm{rand}}$, while matching low-order correlators allows exact minimizers with support coverage as small as $0.07$.
fields.question: Does minimizing classical moment-matching loss functions lead to quantum generative models that generalize rather than merely memorize training statistics?
fields.limits: State-vector simulation up to $N=30$ qubits; tested only on cardinality-constrained and genomic single-nucleotide variant datasets where validity is known.
tools: Direct sample coverage and forward KL divergence benchmarking
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Loss and coverage decouple during training and across model size. (a) IQP at $N=16$ , $\varepsilon{=}0.10$ : the loss (MMD 2 , gray) falls by an order of magnitude while coverage (red) stays near $C_{\mathrm{rand}}$ . (b) a likelihood-trained transformer: the loss (NLL, gray) falls and coverage (blue) rises to the finite-sample maximum $C^{*}$ . (c) coverage versus parameter count at $N=16$ : the classical transformer and RNN and the TNBM rise with size, while IQP and the magic FBM stay near $C_{\mathrm{rand}}$ . (d) normalized coverage $\tilde{C}=C/C^{*}$ versus system size $N$ up to $30$ (raw $C$ is not comparable across $N$ because $|S|$ grows exponentially and the query budget changes with $N$ ): the likelihood-trained and structural models increase toward $\tilde{C}=1$ while IQP holds near $C_{\mathrm{rand}}$ . Throughout, loss is gray and coverage takes each model’s group colour.
fields.figure_gloss: Training loss (gray) and sample coverage (red) plotted across optimization steps and model sizes for IQP Born machines and likelihood-trained classical models. IQP training reduces loss by an order of magnitude while coverage remains flat near the random baseline floor.

fields.result: Calculates exact mean and variance of the quantum neural tangent kernel for degree-$d$ quantum signal processing. Normalized diagonal $3K_d(x,x)/M$ converges in distribution to $\operatorname{Beta}(3/2,1/2)$ with asymptotic coefficient of variation $1/3$, remaining non-self-averaging despite $SU(2)$ Haar mixing.
fields.question: Does a provable training law hold for quantum models when the realized quantum neural tangent kernel is random at initialization and evolves during learning?
fields.limits: Sparse data regime requiring $n^{3/2}(1+\log n)/\sqrt{M} \to 0$ with rescaled time $\tau = Mt/(3n)$ over finite interval $T$; single-qubit model.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Non-self-averaging initialization and angular locality of the mean QNTK. (a) Distribution of the normalized diagonal QNTK $z=3K_{d}(x,x)/M$ at $x=0.6$ . The distributions approach the $\operatorname{Beta}(3/2,1/2)$ law (black). The finite-depth weight above $z=1$ reflects the residual anisotropy of the frame tensor. (b) Exact coefficient of variation $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}K_{d}(x,x)}/\mathbb{E}K_{d}(x,x)$ for three fixed interior inputs. All three curves approach the nonzero asymptotic value $1/3$ (dashed). (c) Along $\alpha+\beta=\pi/2$ , the normalized mean kernel $4\mathbb{E}K_{d}(x,y)/M=\cos^{d}(\alpha-\beta)$ approaches $e^{-u^{2}/2}$ under the rescaling $u=\sqrt{d}\,|\alpha-\beta|$ . The inset shows the corresponding narrowing in the unscaled angular coordinate.
fields.figure_gloss: Diagonal normalized kernel distribution matching the $\operatorname{Beta}(3/2,1/2)$ law (left), coefficient of variation approaching $1/3$ versus depth (middle), and the angular profile of the mean kernel approaching a Gaussian with width $O(d^{-1/2})$ (right).

fields.result: Constructed oracle separations showing Quantum Pessiland: $\mathsf{UP} \cap \mathsf{coUP}$ is strongly hard on average against quantum polynomial-time algorithms with quantum advice, yet auxiliary-input EFI pairs (relative to a quantum oracle) and classically-secure auxiliary-input one-way puzzles (relative to a classical oracle where $\mathsf{SampBQP} = \mathsf{SampBPP}$) do not exist.
fields.question: Is there a quantum analogue of Pessiland where $\mathsf{NP}$ is hard on average but quantum cryptography does not exist?
fields.prior: Wee (2005) constructed classical Pessiland where $\mathsf{UP} \cap \mathsf{coUP}$ is average-case hard but classical one-way functions do not exist; whether quantum cryptography could survive on average-case hard $\mathsf{NP}$ remained open.
fields.limits: Results hold in relativized oracle models (classical and quantum oracle worlds).

fields.result: Linear chain of 6 semiconductor spins with isotropic Heisenberg exchange alone (no $\Delta B_z$) achieves $90.99\% \pm 0.24\%$ test accuracy on full 10,000-image MNIST, reaching $88.1\%$ with linear readout.
fields.question: Can quantum machine learning achieve high expressibility on two-spin units using only isotropic Heisenberg exchange interactions without magnetic field gradients or multi-spin logical encodings?
fields.prior: Classical linear baseline on identical 12 PCA components achieves $83.2\%$, and frozen random exchange dynamics (reservoir) reaches $53.0\%$.
fields.limits: Numerical simulation of 6 spins in the $M_z=0$ subspace; tested against quasi-static pulse-area noise up to $10\%$ and finite shot noise ($10^3$ shots) but without finite-bandwidth charge noise or hyperfine dephasing.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Confusion matrix of the 6-spin TE-EX model on the full MNIST test set (10,000 images, overall accuracy 90.89%). The model successfully distinguishes between the 10 digit classes using only exchange-based dynamics.
fields.figure_gloss: Confusion matrix across all 10 digit classes for the 6-spin TE-EX model on the full 10,000-image MNIST test set, showing an overall accuracy of 90.89%.

fields.result: Unifies projection-test games, Todorov–Turowska projection-lattice games, probabilistic quantum hypergraph games, and graphical rule operators under an operator-bimodule framework, showing winning transformation spaces equal rectangular quantum relations and projection lattices capture precisely the reflexive bimodules.
fields.question: How do disparate formalisms for quantum non-local games mathematically relate to one another at the level of winning rules and game values?
fields.limits: Input and output von Neumann algebras are restricted to finite dimensions; referee algebra $\mathcal{R}$ may be infinite-dimensional.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1. The main quantum-game formalisms compared in this paper through associated operator spaces; $\omega$ -labelled arrows also preserve the value theory.
fields.figure_gloss: Commutative diagram mapping the formal relationships and value-preserving reductions between the various quantum game frameworks via operator spaces.

fields.result: Transverse-field Ising dynamics tune game equilibria via the interaction-time product $Jt$. At $Jt=\pi/2$ (local $iSWAP$ gate), mutual cooperation $(C,C)$ becomes the unique Nash equilibrium across Prisoner's Dilemma, Game of Chicken, and Stag Hunt.
fields.question: How do quantum game equilibria emerge and evolve under continuous Hamiltonian-driven dynamics with tunable entanglement rather than fixed quantum gates?
fields.prior: Gate-based Eisert–Wilkens–Lewenstein (EWL) protocol with fixed entangling operations.
fields.limits: Analyzed for two-player symmetric $2\times 2$ games without environmental decoherence or dissipation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Variation of concurrence with $Jt$ . For $Jt=0$ , $\pi/4$ , $\pi/2$ , concurrence = $0,0.707,1$ respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Concurrence plotted against interaction-time product $Jt$. Entanglement scales monotonically from $0$ at $Jt=0$ to $0.707$ at $Jt=\pi/4$ and reaches unity at $Jt=\pi/2$.

fields.result: Intrinsic residual nuclear spin gradients in isotopically enriched Si/SiGe drive zero-field exchange oscillations, extending singlet coherence from $T_2^* = 1.17 	hinspace	ext{±}	hinspace 0.02	ext{ µs}$ to $T_2^{\mathrm{CPMG}} = 74.8 	hinspace	ext{±}	hinspace 1.8	ext{ µs}$ with $N = 70$ refocusing pulses.
fields.question: Can exchange-coupled semiconductor qubits be characterized at zero applied magnetic field without micromagnets, dynamic nuclear polarization, or multi-axis control calibrations?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a single double quantum dot device; operates within the $S$-$T_0$ two-spin subspace; magnetic shielding below ambient hyperfine field would require modeling $T_{\pm}$ mixing.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Characterization of the double quantum dot device. (a) 2D sweep of exchange pulse $\Delta$ X5 amplitude against wait time in the dephasing (1,1) region, with the $\Delta$ P6, $\Delta$ P5 values set to 0V. The $\Delta$ X5 sweep axis therefore represents a linecut through the exchange fingerprint shown in the inset. For amplitudes that correspond to an odd number of $\pi$ -pulses, a refocusing effect occurs, which results in a Hahn echo-like sequence that extends the singlet coherence time. These refocusing amplitudes are highlighted in the red dashed boxes. For amplitudes that correspond to an even number of $\pi$ -pulses, the exchange pulse has no refocusing effect, effectively turning the experiment into a Ramsey-style sequence, with a correspondingly lower coherence. (b) Calibration of the exchange $\pi$ -pulse by repeating multiple $\pi$ -pulses, while sweeping the $\pi$ -pulse amplitude. Results are normalized across the amplitude rows. Note that a different exchange pulse time was used compared to the measurement shown in (a), resulting in a $\pi$ -pulse occurring at a different $\Delta$ X5 amplitude. From this sequence an optimal $\Delta$ X5 amplitude is chosen, as shown by the white dashed line. The upper panel shows a $\pi$ -pulse train using the optimal $\Delta$ X5 amplitude extracted from (b). (c) CPMG sequence up to N =70 pulses, using the calibrated $\pi$ exchange pulses. A maximum $T_{2}^{\text{CPMG}}$ time of 74.8 $\pm$ 1.8 $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s}$ was extracted. Upper panel shows the pulse sequence used to obtain the CPMG data. The total dephasing time represents the total wait time across the entire CPMG sequence, i.e. $N\times\tau$ . Each curve was fit with an exponential decay function to extract the decay time and normalized between 0 and 1 before plotting. The decay-time uncertainty is estimated as the square root of the corresponding diagonal element of the fit covariance matrix, providing an approximate one-standard-deviation uncertainty under the assumptions of the least-squares model.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured singlet return probability versus total dephasing wait time across CPMG sequences from $N = 0$ to $N = 70$ refocusing pulses, demonstrating coherence extension to $T_2^{\mathrm{CPMG}} = 74.8 	hinspace	ext{±}	hinspace 1.8	ext{ µs}$.

fields.result: Simulated QNDR1 cryoCMOS ASIC achieves SET readout gain of $34.0\text{ MV/A}$ (Version A) and $106.2\text{ MV/A}$ (Version B) with power consumption of $15.9\text{ }\mathrm{\mu W}$ and $13.64\text{ }\mathrm{\mu W}$ in the worst corner.
fields.question: How can a single-electron transistor be DC-coupled and co-designed with cryogenic CMOS amplification circuits to scale SiMOS quantum dot readout without RF components?
fields.prior: Best previous reported readout circuits consume up to $183\text{ }\mathrm{\mu W}$ or require larger layout areas (Gao 2023, Westebring 2024).
fields.limits: Circuit design results are from simulation across 15 corners down to 3.8 K, not direct physical IC measurements.
tools: Periodic steady-state (PSS) and periodic noise (Pnoise) analysis
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 12: Summary of figures of merit compared to selected recent DC-SET readout integrated circuit designs. References in order of appearance: [ 18 ] [ 4 ] [ 19 ] [ 20 ]
fields.figure_gloss: Plots figure of merit, sensing current, area, power, and readout time comparing QNDR1 preamplifier versions against recent literature. Demonstrates lower power, smaller area, and improved figure of merit in simulation.

fields.result: Heavy-hole--light-hole (HH--LH) mixing enables spin--photon strong coupling via LH--LH and LH--HH transitions in flopping-mode germanium double quantum dots, outperforming standard HH--HH transitions in spin--photon figure of merit $r$.
fields.question: Does light-hole admixture produce merely quantitative corrections or open useful alternative channels for coherent cavity coupling in germanium flopping-mode qubits?
fields.prior: HH-only flopping-mode descriptions ignore explicit LH subbands.
fields.limits: Ground-state in-plane orbitals ($j=l=0$) only, truncated 8-state double-dot basis, specified vertical potential well parameters ($d_w = 18\text{ nm}$, $U_{HH} = 100\text{ meV}$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: (a) Ratio $r$ at $\epsilon=0$ and $\Delta_{0}=0$ , defined in Eq. ( 30 ), as a function of magnetic field for the $|0\rangle\rightarrow|2\rangle$ transition in the $U_{LH}=217\penalty\ \mathrm{meV}$ configuration. Values $r>1$ indicate the strong-coupling regime. The curve shows two maxima: the first corresponds mainly to an LH–LH spin-flip transition, while the second corresponds mainly to an LH–HH spin-flip transition. The blue circle marks the maximum value of $r$ , and the right axis shows the cavity frequency required to satisfy the resonance condition at each magnetic field. For the cavity frequency chosen in Fig. 7 , the LH–HH resonance is maximized, blue circle at $B=348\penalty\ $ mT, while the LH-LH transition at that frequency gives $r_{02}\approx 4.14$ , $g_{s,02}/2\pi\approx 3\penalty\ \mathrm{MHz}$ and $\gamma_{s,02}/2\pi\approx 0.22\penalty\ \mathrm{MHz}$ at $B=126\penalty\ $ mT. (b) Spin-photon coupling $g_{s,02}=g_{c}d_{02}$ and effective on-resonance spin-decoherence rate $\gamma_{s,02}$ as functions of magnetic field. The blue circles indicate the values of $g_{s,02}$ and $\gamma_{s,02}$ at the magnetic fields where $r$ is maximized for both the LH–LH and LH–HH transitions.
fields.figure_gloss: Ratio $r$ (panel a), spin--photon coupling $g_{s,02}$ and decoherence rate $\gamma_{s,02}$ (panel b) plotted versus magnetic field $B$ for the ground-to-second-excited state transition at zero detuning. Shows two peaks exceeding the strong-coupling threshold $r>1$, corresponding to LH--LH and LH--HH spin-flip transitions.

fields.result: Numerically decomposes the eigenbasis of arbitrary multi-quantum-dot confinement Hamiltonians into localized single-dot orbital shells ($s, p, d, \ldots$), computing inter-dot tunnel couplings directly as off-diagonal Hamiltonian matrix elements $t^{\alpha\beta}_{ij}$.
fields.question: How to compute localized single-dot orbitals and pairwise tunnel couplings in multi-quantum-dot arrays with arbitrary, biased, or disordered confinement potentials?
fields.limits: Simulations performed for single-particle effective Hamiltonians before Coulomb interaction; assumes spatial segmentation parameter threshold $\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}} \approx 0.9$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Localization algorithm (see End Matter for derivation). (a) Input parameters, determined from the electrostatic confinement potential energy landscape $-e\varphi(\vec{r})$ : Hamiltonian eigenbasis $\left\{\ket{\psi_i}\right\}$ (“ $\psi$ -basis”), and spatial regions $Q^{(\alpha)}$ of distinct QDs obtained from a numerical segmentation algorithm. (b) Decomposition of the vector space spanned by $\left\{\ket{\psi_i}\right\}$ into orthogonal subspaces of states $\left\{\ket{\xi_i^{(\alpha)}}\right\}$ , localized in distinct $Q^{(\alpha)}$ regions. $\vec{C}_{k}^{(\alpha)}$ are the eigenvectors of the overlap matrix $\mathcal{O}^{(\alpha)}$ of the delocalized subbasis, which coincides with the full $\psi$ -basis at first iteration. The eigenvalues $\lambda_{k}^{(\alpha)}$ represent the integrated probabilities of states $\ket{\xi_k^{(\alpha)}}$ within $Q^{(\alpha)}$ . The states with the highest eigenvalues, $\lambda_{k}^{(\alpha)}\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}}$ , are retained for the $\alpha^{\text{th}}$ QD region, whereas the subspace of states with $\lambda_{k}^{(\alpha)}<\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}}$ forms the delocalized basis to be decomposed over other QD regions. The procedure is run sequentially on all $Q^{(\alpha)}$ . (c) The localized $s-,p-,d-,\ldots$ —like orbitals $\left\{\ket{\chi_k^{(\alpha)}}\right\}$ of the $\alpha^{\text{th}}$ QD and their level energies $\epsilon_{k}^{(\alpha)}$ are found by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian projected onto the $\alpha^{\text{th}}$ localized subspace $\left\{\ket{\xi_i^{(\alpha)} }\right\}$ . Tunnel couplings between different localized orbitals are the matrix elements of the full system Hamiltonian in the $\chi$ -basis.
fields.figure_gloss: Decomposition workflow: full Hamiltonian eigenbasis and spatial quantum dot regions are projected onto localized subbases by diagonalizing overlap matrices, yielding localized orbital shells and tunnel couplings.

fields.result: Zero-flux circulating current in triangular triple quantum dots arises via an orbital Hanle effect where dissipative tunneling pumps in-plane orbital pseudospin $\bm{\sigma}$ and noncollinear Lamb shift $\bm{h}$ rotates it to axial chirality $r_z = 2(\bm{h}\times\bm{\sigma})_z/(\gamma^2+4|\bm{h}|^2)$, reversing current when $\bm{h}$ and $\bm{\sigma}$ align.
fields.question: How do voltage-driven circulating currents and scalar spin chirality emerge and reverse in triangular triple quantum dots at zero magnetic flux without complex hopping terms?
fields.prior: Prior work observed bias-induced circulating currents and reversals in triple dots (e.g. Wang et al. 2024), but lacked a microscopic explanation for time-reversal-odd responses from real Hamiltonians.
fields.limits: Ground-multiplet approximation holds at low bias where $w \gtrsim 0.8$; high-bias reversals depart due to contributions from charged/excited states outside the ground space.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Geometric origin of the current reversals. (a) Bias evolution of the normalized Lamb field. (b) Bias evolution of the normalized stationary dissipative pump, with its angle shown in the inset. The marked points identify the two voltages $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ where the vectors become parallel or antiparallel. (c) Their angular factor $\sin(\theta_{\sigma}-\theta_{h})$ , where $\theta_{\sigma}$ and $\theta_{h}$ are their in-plane polar angles. (d) The axial conditional chirality component $r_{z}$ and its ground-multiplet projected current $I_{c}^{(P)}$ in the strong-coupling limit.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots show the bias evolution of the normalized Lamb field $\bm{h}$, dissipative pump $\bm{\sigma}$, their angular alignment $\sin(\theta_\sigma - \theta_h)$, and the resulting axial chirality $r_z$ tracking circulating current reversals at alignment points $V_1$ and $V_2$.

fields.result: Dark mode in a coupled quantum system exhibits effective zero coupling strength and zero Purcell loss to resonator photons, yet maintains a dispersive shift almost identical to bright mode.
fields.question: Can a qubit mode achieve strong dispersive readout shift while completely avoiding Purcell loss?
fields.limits: Relies on higher-order perturbation effects from higher excited states.

fields.result: Spin-to-charge conversion and spin-torque efficiencies in sputtered $\mathrm{Py}/\mathrm{MoTe}_2$ heterostructures remain constant across $\mathrm{MoTe}_2$ thicknesses, demonstrating conversion is driven by interfacial Rashba-Edelstein effect rather than bulk spin Hall effect.
fields.question: Does spin-charge interconversion in sputtered $\mathrm{MoTe}_2$ heterostructures originate predominantly from bulk transport or from the interface?
fields.limits: Room-temperature measurements on sputtered $\mathrm{Py}/\mathrm{MoTe}_2$ thin films.

fields.question: How to generate continuous-variable two-mode binomial cat states without non-Gaussian initial resource states.

fields.result: Exploiting binary-tree decomposition structure reduces inter-module instructions by up to 16.02% over sequential first-fit placement; grid module layouts reduce them by up to 23.7% relative to linear topologies for multi-controlled Toffoli execution via direct $|\mathrm{CCZ}\rangle$ state injection.
fields.question: How can multi-controlled Toffoli gates be efficiently placed and routed on bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity-check modular architectures to minimize inter-module communication overhead and execution error?
fields.prior: was sequential first-fit placement on linear bivariate bicycle code architectures (Yoder et al. 2025)
fields.limits: Ommits magic-state factory distillation error, models circuit failure as independent Poisson-distributed instruction faults, and evaluates error metrics strictly on linear architectures.

fields.result: Encodes compact $U(1)$ lattice gauge fields into one continuous-variable bosonic mode per link by enforcing compactness through a GKP stabilizer, which maps the non-compact line to a circle. Evaluated on a single plaquette, real-time spectroscopy with $\Gamma^2 \to 0$ extrapolation sharpens the extracted charge-induced twist energy from $+1.18\%$ bias at single broadening to $-0.04\%$ relative error ($0.0126316$ vs exact $0.0126361$).
fields.question: How can compact $U(1)$ lattice gauge fields be mapped to continuous-variable bosonic modes without artificial subspace truncation or multi-mode embedding?
fields.prior: Embeds $U(1)$ into pairs of qumodes per link and squeezes onto the circle (Ale et al. 2025).
fields.limits: Validated on classical simulations of single-plaquette $\text{QED}_3$; exact only at infinite squeezing limit ($\Delta \to 0$); requires spectral separation $\Delta_{\rm gap} = \mathcal{O}(1)$ between the twist line and satellite excitations.

fields.result: Introduced dynamic intermediate representation (IR) treating quantum gates as first-class runtime values, enabling dynamic creation, composition, and classical control for hybrid programs within a single framework.
fields.question: How to represent and optimize hybrid quantum-classical programs where gate execution dynamically depends on runtime classical data or measurement outcomes?
fields.prior: Standard static quantum circuit model, which fixes gate sequences and struggles to represent runtime-dependent control and dynamic gate synthesis.

fields.result: Variational optimization of fault-event probabilities via binary cross-entropy on syndrome and logical-flip data learns noise models matching Google Sycamore independently characterized detector error models within $2\%$ in logical error rate.
fields.question: Can quantum error-correction syndrome and logical-observable data collected during memory experiments be used to learn device noise models directly without dedicated characterization runs?
fields.prior: was offline characterization (randomized benchmarking, Pauli channel estimation, sparse Pauli–Lindblad models) requiring separate experiments
fields.limits: Demonstrated on distance-3 surface codes with 3 rounds of syndrome extraction; exact tensor-network contraction scales exponentially with decoding graph treewidth.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : Online noise-model tracking under synthetic device drift for a distance-3 surface code with 3 rounds. The noise model evolves over 20 time steps along a Brownian motion in logit space (Eq. ( 25 )) with drift amplitude $\sigma=0.2$ (left) and $\sigma=0.3$ (right). Five independent random seeds are shown, each as a different color. For each seed, solid lines with circles (“Brownian LER”) show the LER of a decoder with perfect knowledge of the true drifted noise model, while dashed lines with squares (“Learned LER”) show the LER of the online-learned model, which is warm-started from the previous time step. The learned model tracks the true baseline closely across all seeds, even under the larger drift of $\sigma=0.3$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus time step over 20 steps of synthetic Brownian drift in noise parameters for two drift amplitudes. Online warm-started learning matches the baseline of a decoder with perfect instantaneous noise knowledge across five independent runs.

fields.result: For single-qubit blind helper stabilizer codes, helper blindness is necessary and sufficient for recovery via one-way LOCC from the helper. All pure multi-qubit helper codes reduce to a coherent quantum one-time pad undone by a controlled unitary with the helper.
fields.question: What is the general structure and decodability under LOCC of pure quantum secret sharing codes equipped with a privileged helper?
fields.limits: Single-qubit encoded secret. In the stabilizer LOCC-addressable case, requires an odd number of regular parties (unless one party holds multiple shares).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : For a pure QSS scheme, an encoding isometry $W$ allows for the recovery of maximal entanglement with a reference system using the information contained on any authorized subset $S$ of parties.
fields.figure_gloss: Pure quantum secret sharing setup with isometric encoding $W$ and reference system $\widetilde{\mathsf{Q}}$, showing erasure correction and state recovery on any authorized subset $S$.

fields.result: Restricting approximate quantum error correction encoders to rank one incurs an infidelity penalty at most quadratic near perfect recovery, $\Delta \leq (s^{-1}-1)\ell_s(\varepsilon)^2$ for $\varepsilon \leq s$. Higher-rank encoders mapping pure inputs to mixed states are strictly required to attain optimal entanglement fidelity for an explicit noise family arbitrarily close to perfect recovery.
fields.question: Can general, higher-rank encoders strictly outperform partial-isometry (rank-one) encoders in approximate quantum error correction without exact-recovery constraints?
fields.prior: Rank-one encoders lose nothing at exact recovery ($F=1$), but under the earlier bound adapted from Barnum-Knill-Nielsen (1998), replacing an encoder by a partial isometry incurred an infidelity increase up to $\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)$, which is linear in $\varepsilon$.
fields.limits: Bounds assume completely positive trace-non-increasing (CPTNI) or CPTP maps on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with $d_C \geq d_L$; joint optimization is biconvex without analytic global convergence certificates at arbitrary fixed noise.

The black dashed curve is the earlier $\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)$ bound derived from Ref. [ 27 ] . (b) Numerical estimates of the optimized gap versus optimized infidelity for the noise maps constructed below and different values of $d_{L}$ , with $d_{C}=d_{L}^{2}$ . The inset compares the finite-error ratios of the plotted gaps to $(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{opt}})^{2}$ with the asymptotic ceiling $(d_{L}-1)/4$ . The exact limiting coefficient is given by Eq. ( 25 ).
fields.figure_gloss: (a) Infidelity gap bound $\overline{\Delta}(\varepsilon,s)$ plotted against infidelity $\varepsilon$ for various smallest positive eigenvalues $s$, showing the quadratic improvement over the prior $\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)$ bound. (b) Optimized gap plotted against optimized infidelity across varying logical dimensions $d_L$ under a test noise family.

fields.result: Unsupervised representation learning on quantum data requires non-linear data extension maps; joint visible-latent models admitting both inference and generation factorisations exist under the Leifer-Spekkens state-over-time map and are exactly the bipartite states with positive partial transpose (PPT).
fields.question: How can unsupervised representation learning with compatible inference and generation channels be formulated for coherent quantum data lacking a classical probability chain rule?
fields.limits: Restricted to finite-dimensional bipartite systems; excludes non-PPT entangled states from exact Leifer-Spekkens inference and generation.

fields.figure_gloss: Venn diagram showing the nested hierarchy of ambiguous state sets CX-PPT, PPT, and DX-PPT within the space of all bipartite states $S(\mathcal{X \otimes Y})$.

fields.result: Constructed classically verifiable quantum advantage sampling task solvable by $\mathsf{QNC}^0[\log\log]$ circuits (one- and two-qubit gates) or $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits (constant-depth unbounded fan-in gates) with no mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward.
fields.question: Can shallow quantum circuits without mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward demonstrate verifiable quantum advantage under lattice-based hardness assumptions?
fields.prior: LWE-based single-round proof of quantumness of Arabadjieva et al. (2025) operated at higher circuit depth.
fields.limits: Relies on lattice knowledge assumption and a strengthened variant of the adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE; classical hardness is asymptotic.

fields.result: Exact reconstruction of $d$-dimensional channel output observables using physical channels and classical post-processing requires quasiprobability sampling overhead $\nu_1(\operatorname{CPTP}_d) = 2d^2 - 3 + 2/d^2$ for one Choi program copy, and obeys $\nu_k(\operatorname{CPTP}_d) = 1 + (d^2 - 1)/(2k) + o(k^{-1})$ for $k$ copies.
fields.question: Can multiple copies of a physical program state reduce the sampling cost of exact output-observable reconstruction for arbitrary quantum channels?
fields.limits: Product normalized Choi state programs $\pi_{\cal E}^{\otimes k}$; fixed dimension $d$ with $k \to \infty$; shot overhead excludes program preparation, memory lifetime, retriever complexity, and fault tolerance.
tools: semidefinite programming with walled Brauer symmetry
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Exact virtual channel programming. (a) A fixed physical processor with a finite-dimensional program register cannot exactly realize a continuous family of distinct unitary channels. (b) A physical normalized Choi state $\pi_{\cal E}$ selects the target channel for a fixed linear retrieval rule ${\cal P}$ . Its averaged action satisfies ${\cal P}(\rho_{S}\otimes\pi_{\cal E})={\cal E}(\rho_{S})$ at the level of reconstructed output observables. (c) Each trial samples one of the physical channels in a norm-optimal quasi-decomposition ${\cal P}=p_{+}{\cal Q}_{+}-p_{-}{\cal Q}_{-}$ and classically reweights the measured outcome. The total weight $p_{+}+p_{-}=\|{\cal P}\|_{\diamond}$ quantifies the cost of ${\cal P}$ . Minimizing this total weight over exact retrievers defines the programming overhead.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic comparing exact physical channel programming, which is obstructed for continuous families by finite memory, with exact virtual programming using normalized Choi states and norm-optimal quasi-decomposition sampling.

fields.result: Coherent peaks in QDSET and QPC devices separate into two classes: spin-exchange peaks, whose scaling temperature matches $(1/2)\text{FWHM}$, and singlet-cotunneling peaks, which collapse onto $G_{\rm I}(T)$ with exponent $s=0.22$ and have a scaling temperature independent of peak width.
fields.question: Which microscopic spin dynamics dictate the universal scaling functions and peak widths of zero-bias and finite-bias conductance anomalies in quantum dots and quantum point contacts?
fields.limits: Half-filling regime, unidirectional entangled-state tunneling under steady-state non-equilibrium bias.

Red dots and green triangles correspond to a spin-singlet state in the QD, whereas black squares correspond to a spin-triplet state [ 23 ] . The corresponding values of $T_{\rm SC}$ and the data sources are indicated.

fields.question: Can edge transport alone directly resolve the spin structure, coherence, and spin-charge separation of fractional quantum Hall edge states in graphene?

fields.result: Every superconductor adds an interface subband pinned in one of two density classes ($5.3\times 10^{11}\text{ to }6.5\times 10^{11}\text{ cm}^{-2}$ for $d$-band metals; $1.2\times 10^{12}\text{ to }1.3\times 10^{12}\text{ cm}^{-2}$ for Al and Sn), while the buried InAs well keeps its effective mass within 10% and $g$-factor intact.
fields.question: What are the intrinsic semiconductor normal-state parameters beneath a superconducting metal film when electrical transport is shunted by the metal?
fields.limits: Bounds on quantum lifetime $\mu_q$ depend on the assumed transport-to-quantum lifetime ratio $\tau_t/\tau_q \in [1, 4]$; interface state coupling model uses the local wide-band approximation.
tools: InAs/InGaAs heterostructures with Al, Sn, V, Nb, Ta, and Re films

fields.result: Co-designed spin-qubit shuttling bus architecture enables all-to-all logical connectivity via transversal CNOT gates; symmetric shuttling reduces logical error rate by up to 60% compared to asymmetric shuttling at large code distances.
fields.question: How can physical spin-qubit shuttling architectures be co-designed to support both optimized syndrome extraction and low-overhead transversal multi-qubit logical operations?
fields.prior: 1D shuttling-bus architecture optimized via Quantum Reverse Mapping only for single-logical-qubit syndrome extraction (Escofet 2026).
fields.limits: Circuit simulations under phenomenological dephasing and gate-noise parameters without full end-to-end magic state injection noise; based on surface code memory/tCNOT error rates combined via an additive error model.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: Comparison of asymmetric and symmetric shuttling strategies, shown for code distances $d=9$ , $11$ , and $13$ as a function of the number of logical hops. Symmetric shuttling (solid lines) consistently achieves a lower LER than asymmetric shuttling (dashed lines) across all configurations, with improvements of up to $45\%$ , $50\%$ , and $60\%$ for $d=9$ , $11$ , and $13$ , respectively. Inset plots show the improvement percentage as a function of logical hops for each code distance.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate (LER) per transversal CNOT as a function of logical hop distance for code distances $d=9, 11, 13$. Solid lines show symmetric shuttling outperforming asymmetric shuttling (dashed lines) across all distances.

fields.result: Realizes a logical CNOT between distant logical qubits encoded in arbitrary CSS codes using exactly one shared physical Bell pair state $\ket{\Phi^{+}}$ and local gate operations with $O(\log(\tau))$ depth, where $\tau$ is the logical operator support size.
fields.question: Can a remote logical CNOT across monolithic or distributed QPUs be implemented using only a single physical Bell pair instead of a logical Bell pair?
fields.prior: Transversal remote gates, distributed lattice surgery, and gate/qubit teleportation require linear numbers of physical ancillae or logical Bell pairs scaling with code size.
fields.limits: Theoretical design; lacks quantitative numerical fault-tolerance thresholds or error rate simulations; reduced fault tolerance requires containment procedures (intermittent stabilization adding up to $O(\tau_{B} d)$ depth or repetition codes adding ancillae).
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3 : Depth Optimal CNOT for $|B_{X_{L}}|=8$
fields.figure_gloss: Depth-optimal circuit execution for target logical qubit support $|B_{X_{L}}|=8$, achieving logarithmic depth via parallel hierarchical CNOT gates acting on ancilla $q$.

fields.result: Optimal non-adaptive fusion strategy for a single-qubit stabilizer code is given by its largest non-trivial logical operator containing no non-identity stabilizer substring. A perfect fusion strategy exists whenever this operator has full weight, tolerating failure of all but one physical fusion.
fields.question: Which quantum error-correcting codes and non-adaptive measurement bases admit perfect fusion strategies where only a single physical fusion must succeed?
fields.limits: Encodes a single qubit ($k=1$), non-adaptive strategies only, Pauli basis measurements ($X$, $Y$, or $Z$), noiseless/lossless channels with fusion failure as the sole error source.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: An encoded single qubit quantum state undergoes $\sigma$ -fusions for each pair of qubits in $(L,L_{A})$ . The type of each fusion is labeled as a subscript of the blue edges on the leftmost figure. The successful fusions implement a Bell state measurement on the corresponding qubits while a failure implements single qubit measurements in a basis determined by the type of the fusion. If enough fusions succeed then the logical state on $L$ is teleported to $L_{B}$ (depicted on the right side of the figure).
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of single-qubit logical teleportation via physical pairwise fusions between code blocks $L$ and $L_A$, where failed fusions measure single-qubit Pauli observables and successful fusions perform Bell-state measurements.

fields.result: Under uniform circuit-level CZ loss in a compound photon-atom MBQC architecture, periodic RHG achieves the highest threshold at 2.75%. Reduced FFCC surpasses RHG only when excess loss on intermodule CZ connections is sufficiently large.
fields.question: Does reducing MBQC resource graph degree improve error-correction performance under an architecture-aware circuit-level loss model with delayed heralding and correlated bond loss?
fields.prior: Under IID loss, the threshold was approximately 25% for RHG (Barrett & Stace 2010), 8.5% for FFCC, and 13.5% for reduced FFCC (Paesani & Brown 2023).
fields.limits: Simulations under periodic boundary conditions with photon-loss-only error model; atomic loss, dephasing, and photonic Pauli errors are neglected.

The simulations use the circuit-level loss model of Table 1 , with CZ connections designated as intermodule having a loss probability $p_{\mathrm{inter}}=p+q$ instead of $p$ . This modification is applied to the third and fourth CZ connections in RHG and only to the third CZ connection in reduced FFCC. The thresholds $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ are shown for $q\in\{0,p,\ldots,5p\}$ and are extracted from the finite-distance crossings shown in Supplementary Fig. S3 .
