fields.result: Joint entanglement-assisted stabilizer measurements allow remote ebit halves to estimate local phases while attaining the single-qubit quantum Fisher information and identifying $X$-type return errors, leaving the post-sensing state matching the original logical state up to a known Pauli operation.
fields.question: How can remote halves of entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting ebits act as distributed local-phase probes while preserving the encoded logical state for subsequent computation?
fields.limits: Assumes noiseless pre-shared ebits, noiseless Alice-side encoding and storage, ideal stabilizer measurements, and probe noise restricted to independent $X$ errors occurring after phase acquisition.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Exact finite-shot RMSE of the estimator $\hat{\theta}_{j}$ for $M=20$ , $100$ , and $500$ , evaluated under the binomial measurement model. The horizontal dashed lines indicate the corresponding asymptotic levels $1/\sqrt{M}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Root-mean-square error of the estimated phase versus true phase for sample sizes $M = 20, 100, 500$, showing convergence to the asymptotic $1/\sqrt{M}$ shot-noise floor.

fields.result: Average state fidelity decay in dissipative random circuits is universal and independent of dissipative Kraus rank $r$. Decay is completely governed by dissipation strength $\kappa$, qubit number $L$, and circuit depth $T$, while $r$ affects only higher-moment fluctuations.
fields.question: How does the microscopic structure of local dissipative noise affect state fidelity decay in finite-depth random quantum circuits?
fields.limits: Requires random qubit permutation layers and Haar-random distributions for either the two-qubit unitaries or the dissipative Kraus operators.
tools: many-body state fidelity in 4-copy Hilbert space
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Mean fidelity decay for $L=6$ . (a) When either the two-qubit unitaries or the dissipative Kraus operators are sampled from a generic ensemble, the numerical data collapse onto Eq. ( 17 ). (b) In the same scenario than above, the mean fidelity is insensitive to the dissipative Kraus rank $r$ . (c) When both the unitaries and the dissipative component are restricted to free-fermion dynamics, a finite-depth rank dependence remains, but the data approach the generic behavior at larger depth given by the gray dashed line. Notice that the random permutations are implemented as fermionic-mode shuffles via fermionic SWAP decompositions.
fields.figure_gloss: Mean fidelity as a function of circuit depth $T$ for $L=6$ qubits. Data collapse onto theoretical predictions across varying dissipative Kraus ranks $r$, confirming rank independence.

fields.result: Preserving the spatial topology of physical many-body Hamiltonians via a Pauli-gadget intermediate representation reduces compilation overhead to 0.56 $\times$ (two-qubit gates on superconducting platforms), 0.87 $\times$ (infidelity on neutral-atom devices), 0.85 $\times$ (non-Clifford gates on fault-tolerant quantum computers), and 0.75 $\times$ (emitter-entangling operations in measurement-based quantum computing) relative to QuCLEAR.
fields.question: How can quantum compilers preserve the spatial-topology information of many-body Hamiltonians to reduce hardware compilation overhead across diverse quantum architectures?
fields.prior: QuCLEAR compiled Hamiltonians flattened as linear sequences of Pauli strings without hardware-independent topology-preserving intermediate representations.
fields.limits: Evaluated using single second-order Suzuki Trotter steps across four target architectures; structural Hamiltonian inputs set all term coefficients to 1.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 10 . Upper figure: The CNOT count for compilation to IBM quantum computer with heavy-hexagon qubits layout. Lower figure: The CZ count for compilation to Google quantum computer with square-grid qubits layout.
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized two-qubit gate counts across various many-body Hamiltonian benchmark models for compilation targeting IBM heavy-hexagon (CNOT) and Google square-grid (CZ) superconducting layouts.

fields.result: Photonic CSS, GHZ, and arbitrary stabilizer graph states are purified using only linear optics and photon detectors via transversal type-I fusions, reaching per-round success probability up to $1/2$. For 3-qubit (4-qubit) GHZ states under depolarization error $p_{dep}=0.05$, two cascaded rounds raise fidelity from $F\approx 0.86$ ($F\approx 0.81$) to $F=0.988$ ($F=0.981$).
fields.question: How can noisy photonic graph states generated by quantum emitters be purified without deterministic entangling gates?
fields.prior: was $192$ photons on average to produce a 3-qubit GHZ state probabilistically with all-linear optics; emitter-based generation with time-multiplexed two-round purification requires $96$ photons.
fields.limits: Assumes error-free linear-optics circuits. First-order photon loss doubles for small loss rates $p_{l}$ under phase-flip purification.
tools: polarizing beam splitters and photon-number-resolving detectors
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: (a) Fidelities of GHZ states of various sizes after zero (red), one (black), and two (green) purification rounds, assuming depolarization noise with $p_{dep}=0.05$ . For one round, we simulate bit- and phase-flip purification. For two rounds, we consider two cases: one where the phase-flip purification is performed before bit-flip purification (circles), and one where the bit-flip purification is performed before phase-flip purification (stars). (b) Initial fidelities, after one round of phase-flip purification, and after two rounds of purification (phase-flip, followed by bit-flip purification) as a function of $p_{dep}$ . The simulation is performed for a six-qubit GHZ state (crosses) and for a CSS state corresponding to a six-qubit ring graph state (circles).
fields.figure_gloss: GHZ state fidelity plotted against qubit count ($n=2$ to $8$) for depolarization noise $p_{dep}=0.05$ across zero, one (bit- or phase-flip), and two cascaded purification rounds.

fields.result: Recursive module-coupling constructs low-energy subspaces directly from products of module eigenstates on an equal footing without iterative sweeps. Yields variational ground and excited states with computational speedup over DMRG in the moderate-accuracy regime.
fields.question: How can low-energy many-body eigenstates be efficiently computed and hierarchically prepared on gate-based quantum hardware without full-space variational sweeps?
fields.prior: DMRG optimizes global matrix product states through sequential sweeps to obtain excited states one by one.
fields.limits: Accuracy degrades under strong inter-module coupling and hardware noise. Tested on 1D transverse-field Ising chains up to $L=80$ classically and $L=30$ on IBM quantum hardware.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Comparison of the minimum cumulative CPU time required by the modular projected eigensolver and DMRG to reach fixed error-density targets for $J=1.0$ , $g=0.7$ , and $L_{0}=5$ . Panel (a) considers the ground-state energy alone, while panel (b) requires all four lowest energies $E_{0},E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}$ to satisfy the stated error-density threshold. Solid curves with circles correspond to $\epsilon_{\mathrm{tar}}=5\times 10^{-2}$ , and dashed curves with squares correspond to $\epsilon_{\mathrm{tar}}=5\times 10^{-3}$ . All runtime benchmarks were performed using a single CPU thread on an AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor.
fields.figure_gloss: Cumulative CPU time versus system size for the modular projected eigensolver compared to DMRG across target error densities. Panel (a) shows ground-state energy convergence, while panel (b) shows simultaneous convergence for the four lowest eigenstates.

fields.result: Transition-probability interfaces possess continuous blind directions. Adding normalized coherent moment $\widetilde{q}_{-}$ from two-copy interference captures 4-state Bargmann invariants and cuts mean out-of-distribution phase error by 86% at fixed shot budget $N_{\rm tot}=393216$.
fields.question: What information is lost when a quantum representation learner only receives pairwise transition probabilities, and can missing multistate relational invariants be measured and trained directly?
fields.limits: Simulated four-photon benchmark with independent preparation drift; advantage over fidelity baseline relies on fixed two-probe measurement setup unless mode-engineering protects orthogonality ($x_{23}=0$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Direct access to multistate relational observables. (a) A coherent loader prepares the desired pair superposition. (b) The address-controlled overlap operation writes $A_{ij}$ into the $|0^{n}\rangle_{W}$ branch, whose probability gives $p_{-}$ . (c) For two copies, projection followed by a SWAP of one address subsystem yields $q_{-}=\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_{-}^{2}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit sequence for measuring the multistate relational observables: loading pair superpositions into address registers, selecting overlap amplitudes into a target branch to measure $p_{-}$, and measuring two copies with an address SWAP to evaluate second moment $q_{-}=\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_{-}^{2}$.

fields.result: Top-down sequential angle pruning (SAP and objective-aware OSAP) removes $88.8\%$--$92.1\%$ of nonlocal Pauli-string evolutions in multi-angle QAOA while maintaining approximately $95\%$ average fidelity for binary sparse $N=10$ SYK thermofield double states at $\beta=10$.
fields.question: How can gate counts and circuit depth in multi-angle QAOA be systematically reduced while preserving high fidelity for thermofield double state preparation?
fields.limits: Evaluated in classical numerical simulations for $N=8$ and $N=10$ Majorana fermions over 20 disorder realizations; no quantum hardware noise or measurement shot noise modeled.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Infidelity trajectories of the four pruning algorithms for the binary sparse $N=10$ SYK model with $K=16$ at $\beta=0.1$ , $1$ , and $10$ . The curves and shaded regions show $\mathbb{E}_{J}[1-F]$ and $\sigma_{J}[1-F]$ , respectively, averaged over 20 disorder realizations. The black dashed lines indicate the disorder-averaged reference infidelity between the exact TFD state and the maximally entangled state $\ket{I}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Target thermofield double state infidelity $\mathbb{E}_J[1-F]$ plotted against the retained block count $\mathcal{S}$ for the binary sparse $N=10$ SYK model across $\beta = 0.1, 1, 10$. It shows SAP and OSAP maintaining low infidelity down to small block counts compared to batch-pruning baselines.

fields.result: Constructed unitary oracle $U$ separating the classes: $\mathsf{QMA}^{U}\neq\mathsf{QMA}(2)^{U}$. For any $\varepsilon+\delta<1$, any $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-disentangler requires input size exponential in output qubits, resolving Watrous's no-disentanglers conjecture.
fields.question: Can a $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ verifier solve a quantum oracle problem efficiently that no $\mathsf{QMA}$ verifier can?
fields.prior: Unconditional lower bounds held only for $(0,0)$-disentanglers (Aaronson et al. 2009), quasipolynomial bounds for exponentially small $\varepsilon+\delta$ (Harrow, Natarajan, and Wu 2019), or strong disentanglers (Akibue, Kato, and Tani 2025).
fields.limits: Unitary quantum oracle setting (classical oracle separation remains open); asymptotic lower bounds.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : The polynomial degree lower bound we use. Consider a polynomial $p:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying $p(0)=0$ and $1-2^{-(m+1)}\leq p(j)\leq 1$ for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ . Standard approximate-degree bounds for $\mathrm{OR}$ imply that such a polynomial has degree $\Omega(\min\{N,\sqrt{Nm}\})$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Plot of polynomial $p(x)$ versus index $x \in \{0, \ldots, N\}$, showing $p(0)=0$ and $p(j) \approx 1$ for $j \ge 1$, illustrating the approximate degree lower bound reduction to the OR function.

fields.result: One-way puzzles exist if and only if $\mathsf{Gap}\text{-}\mathrm{pK}_{\mathsf{q}}^{t^{*}}$ is weakly quantum-average-hard over quantumly samplable distributions at subexponential time bound $t^{*}(n) = 2^{n/2}\mathrm{poly}(n)$. Any string sampled by a QPT machine with probability $\delta$ admits a description length $\log(1/\delta) + O(\log(nT))$ decodable in time $O(\sqrt{1/\delta}\cdot(nT)^{O(1)})$.
fields.question: Can one-way puzzles be characterized by the average-case hardness of a computable, time-bounded quantum Kolmogorov complexity measure rather than uncomputable plain Kolmogorov complexity?
fields.prior: One-way puzzles were characterized by the average-case hardness of plain, uncomputable Kolmogorov complexity $\mathrm{K}$ ($t=\infty$) over quantumly samplable distributions (Hiroka and Morimae; Cavalar et al.).
fields.limits: Adversaries are restricted to uniform QPT; characterization at polynomial time bounds $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ remains conditional on a conjectured polynomial-time quantum coding theorem.
tools: quantum probability estimation via bitwise extrapolation
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Architecture of the characterization. Black edges are unconditional prior work; blue edges consume a coding theorem, unconditionally supplied at $t^{*}=2^{n/2}\mathrm{poly}(n)$ by Theorem 5.1 and at polynomial time by Conjecture 5.3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Dependency graph showing the reduction cycle between one-way puzzles, exponentially-far non-uniform quantum PRGs, $\mathsf{Gap}\text{-}\mathrm{pK}_{\mathsf{q}}^{t}$ hardness, and quantum probability estimation. Blue edges highlight where the subexponential or conjectured polynomial quantum coding theorems close the equivalence.

fields.result: Calculates a $100\times 100$ gate-voltage charge stability diagram for 64 quantum dots with non-equilibrium latching dynamics in $\sim 0.17\,\mathrm{s}$ on 8$\times$ NVIDIA H100 SXM5 GPUs, scaling polynomially with dot count.
fields.question: How to efficiently simulate both coherent charge hybridization and non-equilibrium latching dynamics in large-scale semiconductor quantum-dot arrays?
fields.prior: Original QArray steady-state solver scaled exponentially and was impractical beyond $\sim 16$ dots; QDarts exceeded 200 s for tunnel coupling at 5 dots.
fields.limits: Simulations assume fixed-size truncated charge bases and short-ranged interdot interactions; timing benchmarks performed on a warm JIT cache with fixed $100\times 100$ pixel scans.
tools: Lindblad master equation (Monte Carlo wavefunction jump trajectory)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Benchmarks for QArray+ on latching, tunnel coupling and Lindblad features. All benchmarks use a 100 × 100 charge-stability-diagram resolution on an 8 × NVIDIA H100 (80 GB HBM3) node. (a) QArray baseline versus QArray+ latching on CPU, single GPU, and 8-GPU, showing that QArray+ on GPU and multi-GPU outperforms the baseline at all dot counts scaling up to 64 dots; multi-GPU maintains sub-second runtimes throughout. (b) Tunnel-coupling benchmark comparing QArray+ (single GPU and multi-GPU) against QDarts, which exceeds 200s at 5 dots while QArray+ remains tractable to 20 dots. (c) Lindbladian benchmark; multi-GPU provides an order-of-magnitude speedup over CPU at 10 dots.
fields.figure_gloss: Computation time per $100\times 100$ charge-stability diagram versus number of quantum dots for latching, tunnel coupling, and open-system Lindbladian solvers across CPU, single GPU, and 8-GPU configurations compared to prior baselines.

fields.result: Local AFM tip-induced strain activates up to six discrete moiré interlayer exciton peaks at room temperature in $\text{MoS}_2/\text{WSe}_2$ heterobilayers, narrowing the dominant peak linewidth from $\sim 38\text{ meV}$ to $\sim 27\text{ meV}$ and tuning emission to $\sim 1.3\,\mu\text{m}$.
fields.question: Can quantized moiré interlayer excitons in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers be resolved, activated, and reversibly tuned at room temperature?
fields.prior: Moiré interlayer excitons were predominantly confined to cryogenic temperatures (e.g. 4 K); room-temperature demonstrations showed only broad, unresolved emission bands without active local control.
fields.limits: Room temperature ($T = 300\text{ K}$), heterobilayers supported on PDMS/glass substrates, maximum tensile strain $\sim 0.5\%$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Activation of moiré IXs by applying tip-induced strain at room temperature. (a) Schematics of the moiré superlattice formed by MoS 2 and WSe 2 monolayers with a twist angle $\theta$ (left), band alignment and IX formation (upper right), and confinement of IX states in the moiré potential (bottom right). (b) Schematic of the experimental configuration, where a MoS 2 /WSe 2 heterobilayer is locally deformed by an AFM tip. (c) Measured PL spectra for an H-type MoS 2 /WSe 2 heterobilayer under varying induced strain increasing from bottom to top. (d–e) PL spectra under the maximum strain from (c) for an H-type (d) and an R-type (e) MoS 2 /WSe 2 heterobilayer, together with fits by six Gaussian functions, demonstrating moiré exciton peaks X1-X6.
fields.figure_gloss: Photoluminescence intensity versus photon energy for $\text{MoS}_2/\text{WSe}_2$ heterobilayers as tip-induced strain increases, resolving six quantized moiré interlayer exciton states (X1–X6) from an initially featureless emission band.

fields.result: Implemented programmable non-Gaussian phase gates $e^{-iV(\hat{X})}$ on a superconducting cavity using bosonic quantum signal processing. Cubic gate produces non-Gaussian states with fidelity $\geq 0.84$ (truncation dimension $D=25$) and Wigner negativity volume $\geq 0.11$.
fields.question: Can arbitrary non-Gaussian phase gates be systematically compiled and tuned on a single continuous-variable hardware template without re-engineering hardware nonlinearities?
fields.limits: Post-selected on qubit remaining in ground state $|g\rangle$. Reconstruction using coherent probes limited to low Fourier harmonics ($|n|\le 2$), requiring squeezed probes for sharp exponential potentials like Morse.
tools: pointwise force reconstruction via coherent-state probes
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Cubic phase gate and non-Gaussian states. (a) The potential and (b) the pointwise force. Target: the programmed potential. Sim: the finite-order compiled circuit carried through coherent-probe sampling and the same deconvolution as the data. The simulated circuit is with unitary qubit-conditioned displacements and qubit rotations, with no decoherence or pulse simulation. Exp: the experimental reconstruction, with shading giving the $95\%$ bootstrap confidence interval in both panels. (c) Output states for coherent inputs at $\langle\hat{X}\rangle_{0}\approx\{-\sqrt{2}/2,\,0,\,+\sqrt{2}/2\}$ . Rows: measured $\mathrm{Re}[\mathcal{C}(\beta)]$ , measured $\mathrm{Im}[\mathcal{C}(\beta)]$ , and Wigner function of the reconstructed density matrix $\rho_{\mathrm{est}}$ . Fidelity against the ideal output state, Wigner negativity volume, and the ideal case are shown inset in each panel.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots of target, simulated, and experimentally reconstructed cubic potential and force versus oscillator position quadrature $\hat{X}$, along with Wigner functions of output states showing negative regions (negativity volume $\ge 0.11$).

fields.result: Demonstrated full fault-tolerant architecture using $[[20,2,6]]$ $C_4$-Helix code on Quantinuum Helios: repeated QEC cycle error of $4.6^{+6.2}_{-2.6}\times10^{-5}$ per logical qubit, two-qubit logical Clifford error of $2.8^{+1.0}_{-1.6}\times 10^{-4}$, and heterogeneous three-logical-qubit GHZ state fidelity lower bound of $99.925^{+0.068}_{-0.245}\%$ without postselection.
fields.question: Can an integrated quantum error-correcting architecture combine compact logical encoding, fault-tolerant transversal Clifford gates, and code-interfacing to outperform unencoded physical baselines on trapped ions?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a trapped-ion hardware architecture; reaching the $10^{-6}$-$10^{-8}$ logical-error regime for early fault-tolerant compute relies on circuit-level simulations with improved physical fidelities.

fields.result: Matrix product state (MPS) optimizations simulate a 15-to-1 magic-state distillation circuit on 187 physical qubits (11 logical qubits, distance $d=3$, 15 logical T gates, hundreds of QEC rounds) with maximal bond dimension 64 in under 40 seconds on 4 CPU cores.
fields.question: Can matrix product states efficiently simulate intermediate-scale quantum error correction circuits with non-Clifford gates in an exact regime?
fields.prior: Near-Clifford simulators PPVM and CAMPS run the same 15-to-1 distillation circuit in 7.9 ms and 47 ms, respectively (~1000 times faster than bare optimized MPS).
fields.limits: Pure state simulation (no non-Clifford noise modeled). Simulation runtime scales exponentially with logical qubit count due to bond dimension $\chi_{\max} = 2^{\lfloor N_L/2 \rfloor + d + 1}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Mean runtimes from random circuits with $N_{L}\in\{3,5,7\}$ logical qubits encoded in a $d=3$ rotated surface code (). Every qubit starts in either $\ket{0}$ or $\ket{+}$ with 50% probability. $n_{\text{gates}}$ random gates drawn from $\{\textsc{H},\textsc{S},\textsc{T},\textsc{CNOT}\}$ are applied with: $n_{\text{T}}=n_{\text{gates}}/4$ T gates, and $p_{\textsc{CNOT}}=0.5$ , $p_{\textsc{H}}=p_{\textsc{S}}=0.25$ for the remaining $3n_{\text{gates}}/4$ gates. The bond dimension at the logical level saturates to the maximum of $2^{\lfloor N_{L}/2\rfloor}$ and at the physical level it is multiplied by 16.
fields.figure_gloss: Simulation runtime versus number of T gates $n_T$ for random circuits on $N_L \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ logical qubits in a $d=3$ rotated surface code. Runtime scales linearly with $n_T$ at constant logical qubit count.

fields.result: Integrated decoding halves required distillation code distance compared to separate decoding, substantially reducing required Bell pairs for distributed quantum error correction primitives under very noisy interconnects.
fields.question: How to synthesize resource-adaptive and context-optimized fault-tolerant distributed quantum error correction primitives when inter-module Bell pairs are much noisier than local gates?
fields.limits: Numerical simulations under circuit-level noise with additional interconnect noise models; applies to surface and color code distributed memories and lattice surgery.

fields.result: Derives a hierarchy of non-decreasing energetic costs for quantum error correction syndrome erasure: $W_\sigma \leq W_{\mathrm{label}} \leq W_{\mathrm{record}} \leq W_{\mathrm{bit}}$, where $W_\sigma$ is lower-bounded by effective syndrome von Neumann entropy $S_{\rm vN}(\sigma)$ and costs decrease with code degeneracy and lower stabilizer check weights.
fields.question: What is the minimal syndrome-related information that must be generated and erased in realistic subspace quantum error correction, and how is its energetic cost constrained by code structure and syndrome extraction?
fields.limits: Subspace codes under local Pauli noise channels. Single-round evaluation without multi-round temporal correlations, decoder retention state conditioning, or full fault-tolerant extraction circuitry.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Erasure work associated with processed syndrome labels for selected stabiliser-code families under independent symmetric local Pauli noise with per-Pauli error probability $p$ . Left: Label-erasure work per physical qubit, $W_{\mathrm{label}}/(Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ , versus code distance $d$ . Degeneracy reduces this quantity by merging physically distinct errors into common recovery labels. Among the families considered, this reduction is most pronounced for the Shor codes, which consequently exhibit the lowest label-erasure work per physical qubit. Right: Total label-erasure work, $W_{\mathrm{label}}/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ , versus the leading-order logical-failure proxy $p_{\mathrm{L}}$ defined in Appendix D , for the same code families and distance range. At fixed $p_{\mathrm{L}}$ , rotated surface codes generally require less total label-erasure work than the corresponding Shor codes. Isolated markers denote the distance-three five-qubit perfect and Steane codes; at the plotted points, they require less total label-erasure work at comparable values of $p_{\mathrm{L}}$ , despite their larger work per physical qubit.
fields.figure_gloss: Label-erasure work per physical qubit $W_{\mathrm{label}}/(Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ plotted against code distance $d$ across various stabilizer code families under symmetric Pauli noise, showing degeneracy-driven energetic reductions.

fields.result: Frequency-multiplexed parallel entangling gates on a 512-ion 2D crystal implement a $[[248,10,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code at a logical error rate of $10^{-12}$ using peak per-ion Raman Rabi rates of $2\pi \times 0.99\text{ MHz}$ (conservative noise) and $2\pi \times 0.29\text{ MHz}$ (aggressive noise).
fields.question: Can parallel nonlocal entangling gates be executed on a large 2D ion crystal without physical shuttling while suppressing crosstalk errors and remaining robust to experimental noise?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation of a 512-ion crystal; assumes counter-propagating $355\text{ nm}$ Raman beams on ${}^{171}\text{Yb}^{+}$, trap frequency drift $\Delta\omega/2\pi$ between $\pm 100\text{ Hz}$ and $\pm 500\text{ Hz}$, $T_2$ coherence of $1\text{--}3\text{ s}$, and single-qubit gates are ideal.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Performance of BB18 code on a 2D crystal of $N=512$ ions. (a) Total entangling gate time per syndrome-measurement cycle vs. peak per-ion Rabi rate $2\sum_{k}\Omega_{k}/N$ for different scheduling of the parallel gates. (b) Logical error rate per syndrome-measurement cycle vs. peak per-ion Rabi rate $2\sum_{k}\Omega_{k}/N$ . We consider two representative sets of noise parameters. A more conservative set (red circles) assumes a trap frequency drift $\Delta\omega/2\pi=\pm 500\,$ Hz, a spin dephasing time $T_{2}=1\,$ s, an average phonon number $\bar{n}_{m}=1$ for each drumhead phonon mode, and a measurement error of $p_{\mathrm{meas}}=10^{-3}$ . A more aggressive set of parameters (green circles) uses $\Delta\omega/2\pi=\pm 100\,$ Hz, $T_{2}=3\,$ s, $\bar{n}_{m}=0.1$ and $p_{\mathrm{meas}}=5\times 10^{-4}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate per syndrome-measurement cycle (b) and total entangling gate duration (a) plotted against peak per-ion Raman Rabi rate $2\sum_k \Omega_k/N$ for different parallelism levels under conservative and aggressive noise parameters.

fields.result: Constructs quantum low-density lattice codes (qLDLCs) and decodes concatenated GKP-LDPC codes with fully analog, linear-time iterative message-passing decoders. After dimensionality reduction to a single qubit, a 15–17-mode qLDLC achieves a lower logical error rate than a 25-mode ($5\times 5$) hexagonal GKP-surface code under low Gaussian displacement noise.
fields.question: Can classical low-density lattice code constructions and analog message-passing decoders be adapted to continuous-variable GKP codes to avoid the hardness of closest-vector decoding?
fields.limits: Dimensionality reduction introduces two non-sparse checks causing short cycles; convergence analysis from classical LDLCs does not directly apply to irregular quantum Tanner graphs; simulations assume additive white Gaussian displacement noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Dimension-reduced GKP-LDLC codes compared to surface-code baselines. (a) Euclidean distances of randomly generated GKP-LDLC codes after reducing the logical dimension to a single qubit as explained in Section III.2 . For each instance we plot the three logical distances $\Delta_{X}$ (circles), $\Delta_{Y}$ (squares) and $\Delta_{Z}$ (diamonds); all three are inequivalent because the reduced code is no longer CSS. Note that which displacements correspond to $X,Y,Z$ logicals is arbitrary, so here we sorted them for increasing distance for visual clarity. Instances are grouped by the number of modes $n$ . Horizontal lines mark the distances of rotated surface codes concatenated with the single-mode square GKP code and hexagonal GKP code. (b) Logical error probability $P_{L}$ of the reduced GKP-LDLC codes under an isotropic Gaussian displacement channel of standard deviation $\sigma$ , estimated by Monte-Carlo nearest-point (CVP) decoding on the dual lattice. Solid lines with filled markers are GKP-LDLC codes; dashed lines with open squares are rotated surface codes concatenated with the hexagonal single-mode GKP code, matched by mode number.
fields.figure_gloss: Euclidean code distances and logical error rates under Gaussian displacement noise comparing single-qubit dimension-reduced GKP-LDLCs against mode-matched hexagonal GKP-surface codes.

fields.result: Estimates effective layer polarization $p_{\mathrm{eff}}$ by measuring state overlap $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_A \rho_B)$ across identical random circuits on two disjoint registers as a function of depth, avoiding classical simulation and reference state recovery. Clear exponential decay verified experimentally on 8-qubit and 16-qubit registers.
fields.question: How to design a scalable circuit-level benchmark that supports universal non-Clifford gate sets without requiring classical output simulation, state inversion, or subsystem partitioning?
fields.limits: Requires randomized compiling or Pauli twirling to capture fixed coherent errors; inter-register correlations introduce an additional covariance contribution to measured overlap.
fields.figure_caption: (a) Swap test
fields.figure_gloss: Three quantum circuit schematics: overlap measurement via swap test using an ancilla, pairwise Bell-basis measurement on register pairs, and the full EPCL sequence applying identical random circuit layers to two disjoint registers before overlap readout.

fields.result: Parity Twine Networks adapted to neutral-atom hardware reduce two-qubit gate count, atom shuttling, and depth, yielding estimated circuit fidelity three orders of magnitude higher for a 30-qubit quantum Fourier transform.
fields.question: How to optimize gate count, circuit depth, and atom shuttling for the Parity Architecture on neutral-atom quantum processors with diverse native gates and geometries?
fields.prior: Prior compilation strategies achieved lower estimated fidelity (three orders of magnitude lower for 30-qubit QFT).
fields.limits: Estimated fidelities derived from analytical/numerical resource counts rather than physical execution on hardware; applies to circuits encoding interactions in a common basis.
tools: Native CZ, CZSWAP, and iSWAP gate realizations

fields.result: Training parameterized quantum models without classical optimization or gradient estimation by mapping parameters to quantum degrees of freedom and evolving them under a loss Hamiltonian via block encodings, concentrating probability amplitudes at low-loss configurations.
fields.question: Can quantum learning models be trained entirely through coherent unitary evolution without classical parameter optimization loops?
fields.limits: Numerical simulations restricted to 2-parameter classification with 5 qubits per parameter ($2^5$ grid points) and 1-parameter phase estimation ($n=5$ qubits, 32 grid points). Assumes fault-tolerant query access to block encodings.
fields.figure_caption: (a) Dataset employed in the numerical simulations. The task is a one-dimensional binary classification problem in which samples lying inside the interval $\left(-\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ are assigned to one class, while the remaining samples belong to the other class. Noise is added to the data. The training and test sets contain 100 and 500 samples, respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Training and test loss as a function of updates on a 1D binary classification dataset with 100 training and 500 test samples. CQL matches the convergence of hybrid stochastic gradient descent within approximately 15 updates.

fields.result: Defines abstract quantum data types in universal algebra and establishes that equational specifications soundly lift from classical to quantum data types under bit-oracle and phase-oracle quantisations. Determines exact conditions for quantisation to preserve structural embeddings, isomorphisms, and Cartesian/tensor products.
fields.question: How can we realize data abstraction in quantum programming and systematically lift classical abstract data types to the quantum setting?
fields.limits: Only covers finite data domains, purely quantum data types without classical-quantum hybrid interactions or measurements, and unitary operations specified via bit and phase oracles.
tools: bit oracle and phase oracle quantisation

fields.result: Classical $\mathcal{O}(|V|^2)$ vertex partition refinement on tree graphs determines whether standard symmetry-reduced QAOA matches the multi-angle reduced DLA, certifying pure-state or subsystem controllability and establishing explicit lower bounds $\dim(\mathfrak{g}^v_{\Gamma,\mathrm{std}}) \geq \dim(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma',\mathrm{free}})$.
fields.question: Given a particular symmetry reduction, can we efficiently determine what quantum dynamics it generates without explicitly recovering the reduced DLA?
fields.prior: Direct calculation of the dynamical Lie algebra via repeated commutations scales exponentially with qubit count.
fields.limits: Restricted primarily to connected acyclic graphs (trees), with generalizations requiring unique shortest paths (geodetic graphs).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Overview of results and symmetry-reduction framework. In the presence of a global bit-flip symmetry, fixing the bit value at any chosen reference vertex $v$ yields a reduced optimization problem equivalent to the original, along with a reduced QAOA ansatz and its corresponding reduced dynamical Lie algebra. A canonical example exhibiting this symmetry is the MaxCut problem, which serves as the primary focus of this work. (Bottom) We present a polynomial-time classical algorithm with computational complexity $\mathcal{O}(|V|^{2})$ that partitions the vertices of connected acyclic graphs based on their shortest-path distances to a chosen reference vertex $v$ and the vertex degree parities along those paths. Selecting different reference vertices $v$ induces distinct partitions, leading to two operational regimes: (Left) Partial refinement: certifies subalgebra inclusions, establishing rigorous lower bounds on the reduced DLA dimension and guaranteeing conditional subsystem reachability. (Right) Full refinement: identifies the reduced DLA; pure-state controllability follows under the conditions of Section V .
fields.figure_gloss: Overview of the symmetry-reduction workflow for MaxCut QAOA on trees, showing how fixing a vertex bit reduces circuit size and determines the reduced dynamical Lie algebra via graph-structure refinement.

fields.result: Sparse Clifford phase circuits with independent local single-qubit Clifford twirling form $\epsilon$-approximate projective $2$- and $3$-designs with vanishing relative error. The design can be realized in quantum depth seven using $O(n\log(n/\epsilon))$ ancilla qubits with adaptive measurements and feedforward, or in ancilla-free depth $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$.
fields.question: Can constant-depth quantum architectures realize quantum projective designs with vanishing relative error?
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime in qubit number $n$, projective state designs for $k=2$ and $k=3$, all-to-all connectivity.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Schematic illustration of random circuit ensemble. (a) Structural contrast between our shallow phase-circuit construction (left) and generic shallow random circuits based on ”gluing” non-commuting $O(\log n)$ -qubit patches [ 12 ] or non-commuting local bricks [ 15 ] (right). (b) Our moment analysis makes the deviation from Haar transparent. For example, at second order, the relative-error obstruction is carried by the residual term $\Delta_{2}^{\otimes n}$ . Local Clifford twirling maps $\Delta_{2}$ to $\widetilde{\Delta}_{2}$ , exponentially suppressing this contribution, as quantified around Eq. 3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic comparing the proposed shallow commuting phase architecture with standard brickwork circuits, and diagram showing suppression of relative-error deviations under local Clifford twirling.

fields.result: Discretization-aware fine-tuning (DAFT) reduces BBBP cross-class bit collisions from 11544 to $\approx 1$, raising 10-qubit quantum classifier accuracy by $+12.2\,\mathrm{pp}$ to 0.883 and beating an identically-discretized classical logistic regression by $+2.8\,\mathrm{pp}$ ($p=0.026$).
fields.question: How can continuous representations from classical foundation models be adapted to prevent label-destroying collisions when discretized into small quantum registers for bit-bit QML?
fields.prior: Without DAFT, frozen ChemBERTa-77M embeddings produced 11544 collisions and 10-qubit quantum circuits trailed the matched classical bit-string baseline by $-6.0\,\mathrm{pp}$ (0.762 vs 0.822).
fields.limits: Evaluated on BBBP binary molecular classification dataset up to $n_q=10$ qubits; quantum simulation setting.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 1: Pipeline overview. SMILES strings are mapped to embeddings by ChemBERTa-77M. The baseline (blue) uses frozen embeddings, while the proposed method (purple) applies discretization-aware fine-tuning (DAFT). Both paths share the same preprocessing pipeline (standardization, PCA, mutual information selection, and quantization) to produce bit-string inputs for the quantum circuit. All classical baselines are evaluated on identical inputs for fair comparison.
fields.figure_gloss: End-to-end pipeline mapping SMILES strings via ChemBERTa-77M and DAFT fine-tuning, standardized/quantized to bit-strings, and fed into quantum and classical baselines.

fields.result: No finite classical communication can exactly simulate quantum communication or entangled-pair Bell correlations for dimension $d_Q \ge 4$. For qutrits ($d_Q = 3$), an explicit protocol simulates all states and measurements using $357$ classical bits.
fields.question: Can the statistics of $d$-dimensional quantum communication and Bell correlations across all measurements be exactly simulated with a finite amount of classical communication and shared randomness?
fields.prior: Qubits ($d_Q = 2$) were known to require and suffice with $2$ classical bits (Toner and Bacon 2003). For $d_Q \ge 3$, only lower bounds were known: $C_{\mathrm{cl}}(3) \ge 5$ and $C_{\mathrm{cl}}(4) \ge 10$.
fields.limits: Exact classical simulation with unlimited shared randomness; single-round classical communication; exact reproduction of all POVMs and quantum states.
tools: complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^3$ and $\mathbb{CP}^2$ geometric analysis
fallback protocol and acceptance rejection sampling
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Classical simulation of quantum communication and Bell nonlocality. (a) In the communication setting, a quantum state $\rho$ of dimension $d_{Q}$ is communicated to a measurement device. Given a measurement $M$ , an outcome $b$ is produced with probability $p_{Q}(b\mid\rho,M)$ . In a classical simulation, the quantum system is encoded in a message $c$ of finite dimension using unlimited shared randomness, and decoded producing $b$ with probability $p_{C}(b\mid\rho,M)$ . A classical simulation exists if there is an encoder and decoder functions realizing $p_{C}(b\mid\rho,M)=p_{Q}(b\mid\rho,M)$ for all possible inputs $\rho$ and $M$ . (b) In the Bell nonlocality setting, a quantum state $\rho_{AB}$ is shared between two experimenters, who locally measure their systems with $M^{A}$ and $M^{B}$ , producing the outcomes $a,b$ with probability $p_{Q}(a,b\mid M^{A},M^{B})$ . A classical simulation replaces the shared quantum state with unlimited shared randomness and allows a message $c$ of finite dimension to be communicated between the devices. The simulation exists if $p_{C}(a,b\mid M^{A},M^{B})=p_{Q}(a,b\mid M^{A},M^{B})$ for all possible $M^{A}$ and $M^{B}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic setup for classically simulating single-party $d_Q$-dimensional quantum state transmission (a) and bipartite entangled Bell nonlocality (b) via classical message $c$ and shared randomness $\lambda$.

fields.result: Collective one-axis-twisting dynamics driven by pulsed magnetic-field gradients and dressed-state encoding achieve metrological gains of up to 7.9(2) dB for magnetic signal detection and 8.8(3) dB for magnetic noise sensing.

fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Signal amplification through collective many-body dynamics. a, Experimental sequence realizing signal amplification. The spin ensemble is optically polarized at zero magnetic field, after which the perpendicular field $B_{\perp}$ is ramped to $362.4~\mathrm{G}$ to tune the dipolar interaction to the form of Eq. ( 1 ). A MW pulse of angle $\theta=\pi/2\pm\delta\theta$ mimics the sensing signal, followed by an OAT stage that amplifies the encoded response. The OAT dynamics are implemented through pulsed control of magnetic-field gradients and MW drive [ 8 ] : a conical spin spiral is wound, evolved under a generalized (XY8) m sequence that decouples on-site disorder, and then unwound at the end of the quench. An optional MW turn pulse $\alpha_{k}$ enables multi-stage amplification, for which the “OAT+turn” sequence is repeated $n$ times. The OAT-generating wavevector is alternated between $+Q$ and $-Q$ in odd/even amplification stages, for suppressing decoherence (see Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplement). The global spin state is finally read out by ramping $B_{\perp}$ back to zero and measuring the fluorescence under laser illumination. In practice, the ramping of $B_{\perp}$ is achieved by turning on an auxiliary pulsed magnetic field during initialization and readout (Methods), which temporarily cancels the bias field $B_{\perp}$ . b, Measured polarization dynamics at polar angle $\theta=45^{\circ}$ , demonstrating high-quality collective OAT dynamics. c, Measured twisting rate $\omega$ and transverse decay rate $\gamma$ as a function of spiral wavevector at polar angle $\theta=45^{\circ}$ . Solid curves show predictions from the system model (Methods). d, Measured dynamics for a pair of initial states with sensing angle $\theta=90\pm 3^{\circ}$ , demonstrating amplification of a small signal. Black arrows indicate the turn pulse used for multi-stage amplification, after which faster twisting dynamics lead to larger amplification. e, Measured distance (in units of the Bloch-sphere radius) between the initial-state pair in d as a function of total many-body evolution time, for single-stage ( $n=1$ ) and multi-stage ( $n=2,3$ ) protocols. The point at $t=0$ corresponds to the initial distance $2\mathrm{sin}\left(3^{\circ}\right)\approx 0.105$ . Errors represent 1 s.d. accounting statistical uncertainties.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured spin polarization dynamics, twisting/decay rates, and separation distance showing up to 5.4x signal amplification via multi-stage collective one-axis twisting.

fields.result: Deterministic vertical-to-vertical transfer of InAsP/InP nanowire quantum dots via electron-beam-induced deposition of $\mathrm{SiO}_x$ nano-glue onto pre-fabricated templates. fields.question: Can vertical nanowire quantum dots be deterministically transferred to pre-patterned templates without losing their upright geometry, optical quality, or single-photon purity?
fields.prior: Nanowire quantum dot pick-and-place transfer relied on van der Waals forces limited to lying-down geometries, while as-grown upright nanowires had a maximum top extraction efficiency limit of 50%.
fields.limits: Demonstrated across 8 transferred nanowire devices on mirror templates; Stark tuning tested up to 120 V across a 600 nm gap; spectral shift is reduced compared to theory likely due to screening from background doping in the nanowire.

fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Syndrome-extraction schedule comparison for twelve planar distance-11 surface-code patches and three implementations of the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (BB) code: LR-triangular, LR-planar, and systolic. fields.result: Proves optimal root-influence inequality $\|p\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\ge \sum_i \sqrt{\mathrm{Inf}_i[p]}/t$ for degree-$t$ block-multilinear polynomials, and tight top-level Fourier growth $\|\widehat{p}_{2t}\|_{\ell_1} \le (en/(2t-1))^{\frac{2t-1}{2}} \|p\|_{\mathrm{cb}}$ for degree-$2t$ polynomials.
fields.question: Can inequalities for completely bounded polynomials establish improved upper limits on the computational power and Fourier growth of quantum query algorithms?
fields.prior: Root-influence bound was $\|p\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\ge \sum_i \sqrt{\mathrm{Inf}_i[p]}/t^2$ (Bansal, Sinha, and de Wolf 2022).
fields.limits: Applies to quantum query algorithms whose acceptance probabilities or amplitudes map to completely bounded polynomials (e.g. block-multilinear architectures, parallel query models).
tools: Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube
operator norm bounds on tensor forms
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Quantum query algorithm that queries disjoint blocks of variables $x_{1},\dots,x_{t}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit schematic with $t$ sequential queries applied to disjoint input blocks $x_1, \dots, x_t$, interleaved with unitary operations.

fields.result: Introduced chameleon gates $\mathcal{C}_{\rho}$ parametrized by a quantum state knob $\rho$, constructible via a controlled-$\mathrm{swap}$ and partial trace to implement state-based quantum computation and simulate nonlinear Hamiltonians.
fields.question: How can quantum controlled-gates be generalized to adapt their transformations dynamically based on arbitrary input quantum states without prior knowledge of those states?
fields.limits: Requires ancilla control qubit initialized with small parameter $|δ| \ll 1$; valid up to $O(\delta^2)$ error; requires post-selection on the $|+\rangle$ measurement outcome.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: [Left] Quantum-circuit schematic of a state-based controlled-gate $\mathcal{C}_{\rho}$ , which we refer to as the chameleon gate [Eq. ( 6 )]. [Right] An equivalent standard gate-based construction is also shown for this gate, which uses a specific combination of quantum states, quantum controlled- swap gate, and partial tracing. Note that basically the control qubit can be any state. But when the control qubit is chosen as $\psi_{\delta}$ with $|\delta|\ll 1$ , this also yields an implementation for $\mathpzc{U}_{\rho}$ [Eq. ( 1 )] to an $O(\delta^{2})$ error.
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit schematic for the chameleon gate $\mathcal{C}_{\rho}$ and its implementation using an ancilla in state $\psi_\delta$, a state knob $\rho$, target state $\sigma$, controlled-swap, and partial tracing over the first target.

fields.result: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas (L-MPF) combine classically computed linear coefficients with noisy quantum expectation values to outperform low-bond-dimension classical tensor network simulations and unmitigated quantum results on 65 qubits, achieving classical GPU speedups up to $5.6\times$.
fields.question: Can high-dimensional tensor network contractions be integrated directly into a quantum error mitigation workflow to estimate noiseless expectation values with rigorous error bars?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a 2D discrete time crystal model on a $3\times 3$ heavy-hexagonal lattice up to 10 Floquet cycles; non-ergodic amplification settings require PEA and higher sample counts to prevent large error bars.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Comparison of dimensionless expectation values obtained with three methods: (i) purely classical high bond dimension simulations, (ii) purely classical low bond dimension simulations that have been extrapolated to the zero truncation error limit, and (iii) quantum hardware results on ibm_basquecountry that have been mitigated with the L-MPF method, where the expectation values in the sum $c_{i}\langle O\rangle_{\lambda_{i}}$ have been obtained with ergodic amplification. a) Expectation values of the target observable, with corresponding $1\sigma$ error bars, shown as a function of the Floquet cycles. The reference expectation values (black) are obtained from Schrödinger-picture tensor network simulations with a truncation error of $10^{-8}$ . The red markers correspond to the application of the L-MPF workflow to the raw hardware measurements, while the noiseless expectation values (blue) are extrapolated from Heisenberg-picture tensor network simulations. b) Deviation from the Schrödinger-picture belief propagation expectation values for both Heisenberg-picture simulation and hardware values, shown as a function of the Floquet cycles. The blue and red markers correspond to the same datasets shown in plot a), and the shaded regions indicate the associated $1\sigma$ error bands. Details regarding the calculation of these uncertainties are discussed in the main text.
fields.figure_gloss: Expectation value vs. Floquet cycle number, comparing purely classical low-bond simulations, unmitigated hardware measurements, and L-MPF error-mitigated results against high-bond-dimension classical ground truth.

fields.result: Dual-space NOCI variationally couples a parent reference manifold to generated correlated quantum states, bounding the Rayleigh–Ritz energy at or below both reference-only NOCI and correlated-only NOQE while reducing sensitivity to amplitude and matrix-element noise.
fields.question: How can quantum subspace eigensolvers augment a classical nonorthogonal configuration interaction reference without degrading variational flexibility when correlated quantum states are incomplete or noisy?
fields.limits: Simulated benchmarks on small molecules ($H_2$, $H_4$, $H_6$, $N_2$, cyclobutadiene); noisy matrix elements degrade the strict variational bound without metric regularization.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Error relative to FCI for the correlated space only NOQE and DS-NOCI descriptions of linear H 4 /STO-3G at $R=2.0$ bohr as a function of Gaussian perturbations to the MP2 doubles amplitudes. Markers denote the mean over 200 realizations and error bars indicate the standard deviation.
fields.figure_gloss: Energy error relative to FCI for linear $H_4$ plotted against amplitude noise variance $\sigma$. DS-NOCI retains stable accuracy while correlated-only NOQE error degrades rapidly.

fields.result: Demonstrated ancilla-mediated reservoir engineering on a solid-state spin pair, realizing anti-thermalization to a negative-temperature steady state and achieving quantum battery steady-state ergotropy exceeding 70% of theoretical maximum after 30 collisions.
fields.question: Can an ancilla qubit be used to engineer tunable system-reservoir coupling and reservoir temperature to achieve anti-thermalization and non-equilibrium steady states?
fields.limits: Natural $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ abundance Type IIa diamond at room temperature; NV-nuclear spin correlations assumed weak and ignored across cycle boundaries.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Simulated (solid/dashed) and experimental (markers) system energetics: (a) Coherent evolution of the excited - state population of $S$ , $p_{S,\uparrow}$ , under the reversible channels $H^{+}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (yellow) and $H^{-}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (red), shown for inter - pulse delays of $376$ ns (dashed) and $370$ ns (solid) as a function of $N$ (see Fig. 2 ). (b) Thermalisation of $S$ under $H^{-}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ for hot and cold baths at $370$ ns (solid) and $376$ ns (dashed) and N $=8$ as function of collision number, $\kappa$ . (c) Anti - thermalisation under $H^{+}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ , including a lighter trace for driving at $365$ ns. (d) Dynamics of system coherence $\mathcal{C}_{S}$ (solid) and quantum correlations (dashed), quantified via Negativity $\mathcal{N}_{AS}$ and Mutual Information $\mathcal{I}_{AS}$ for inter-pulse delay of $370$ ns and N $=8$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Excited-state population dynamics and energetics of the nuclear spin system qubit undergoing collisions under engineered interaction channels.

fields.result: Residual $ZZ$ interaction cancels completely outside straddling regime without direct qubit-qubit capacitive coupling using single-junction double-resonator coupler. Provides $\sim 70\,\mathrm{MHz}$ activated $ZZ$ interaction, enabling $20\,\mathrm{ns}$ CZ gate with simulated coherent infidelity below $10^{-5}$.
fields.question: How to completely suppress residual $ZZ$ interactions across flexible qubit-qubit frequency detunings without requiring multi-junction couplers or direct capacitive layout constraints?
fields.prior: Single-transmon couplers require qubit detuning within straddling regime and direct qubit capacitance balancing; double-transmon and fluxonium couplers require multiple Josephson junctions.
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only. Evaluated using a 20-state basis with perturbative leakage corrections; dephasing assumes $1/f$ flux-noise amplitude $A_{\varphi_{\mathrm{ex}}}=2\pi\times 10^{-6}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Circuit diagram of the proposed architecture. Two transmon qubits, $\mathrm{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{Q}_{2}$ (purple), are capacitively coupled to a double-resonator coupler (DRC, blue). (b) False-color rendering of the device layout, with colors matching the circuit elements in (a). The scale bar denotes $200\,\mu$ m. (c) Mode-coupling diagram of the qubit–DRC system, with arrow colors indicating the coupling signs: red (blue) denotes positive (negative) coupling. The common mode $\Sigma$ couples positively to both qubits, whereas the differential mode $\Delta$ couples negatively to Q 1 and positively to Q 2 . Asymmetric inductance values ( $L_{\ell}\neq L_{r}$ ) introduce an inter-mode coupling $g_{L}$ between the $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$ modes. (d) Single-excitation spectrum of the qubit–DRC system versus reduced external flux $\varphi{\mathrm{ex}}$ . Dotted curves show the coupler eigenenergies in the symmetric limit $\Delta E_{L}=0$ ( $g_{L}=0$ ), dashed curves show the bare eigenenergies of $\hat{H}{\mathrm{q}}+\hat{H}{\mathrm{c}}$ for $\Delta E_{L}/h=-16~\mathrm{GHz}$ , and solid curves show the dressed eigenenergies of the full Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ . The labels $\ket{n_{1}n_{2};n_{\Sigma}n_{\Delta}}$ denote bare states with occupations $n_{1},n_{2}$ in the qubits and $n_{\Sigma},n_{\Delta}$ in the common and differential modes. (e) Differential-mode potential and wavefunctions at selected external flux biases $\varphi_{\mathrm{ex}}/2\pi=0$ , $0.3$ , and $0.5$ . The gray-to-black curves show the potential energy as a function of $\varphi_{\Delta}$ , and the colored curves show the wavefunctions of the three lowest eigenstates $\ket{n}_{\Delta}$ ( $n=0,1,2$ ), each offset vertically by its eigenenergy. (f) Schematic of the coupler-mediated exchange interaction. Tuning the differential-mode frequency $\omega\Delta$ through the common-mode frequency $\omega_{\Sigma}$ changes the relative strengths of the two virtual exchange paths, tuning the effective qubit–qubit coupling $\tilde{g}_{12}$ from positive to negative and producing cancellation near $\omega_{\Delta}\simeq\omega_{\Sigma}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit and layout of transmon qubits coupled via the double-resonator coupler (a, b), mode coupling and flux-dependent single-excitation spectra (c, d), differential-mode potential wells (e), and mechanism of virtual-exchange path cancellation (f).

fields.result: Electrostatic splitting of an edge magnetoplasmon resonator yields RF transmission signatures for integer ($\nu=1, 2$) and fractional ($\nu=4/3, 2/3$) quantum Hall states, with cavity perimeter dropping to $17.5\text{ }\mathrm{\mu m}$ past QPC pinch-off.
fields.question: How does polarizing an embedded quantum point contact influence edge magnetoplasmon modes and cavity geometry in a quantum Hall resonator?
fields.limits: Aharonov-Bohm interference oscillations not observed due to small expected period; $\nu=2/3$ center field was beyond maximum accessible magnetic field ($B > 8\text{ T}$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Integrated amplitude along resonance: From full $(f,B)$ transmission maps we can fit the $1/B$ decrease of the resonance frequency for each value of the QPC voltage. By integrating over a $200\text{\,}\mathrm{MHz}$ frequency window around the central resonance frequency we obtain the following figure that show the resonances associated to the various quantum Hall plateaus as a function of the QPC voltage and magnetic field. For each value of $V_{\mathrm{QPC}}$ we extract the position of the integer plateaus ( $\nu=2$ for $V_{\mathrm{QPC}}>-0.5$ and $\nu=1$ for $V_{\mathrm{QPC}}<-0.6$ ) and extrapolate to the expected position of other integer and fractional plateaus shown with dot markers.
fields.figure_gloss: Averaged RF transmission amplitude $\langle|Z|^2\rangle$ plotted against QPC gate voltage $V_{\mathrm{QPC}}$ and perpendicular magnetic field $B$. Peaks trace resonance trajectories for integer $\nu=1, 2$ and fractional $\nu=4/3, 2/3$ Hall plateaus across the QPC pinch-off transition.

fields.result: Single-qubit average Clifford fidelity reaches $99.61\% \pm 0.03\%$ and two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen Bell-state fidelity reaches $92.35\% \pm 1.50\%$ using a chip-scale Brillouin laser locked to an integrated coil resonator.
fields.question: Can an integrated visible-wavelength narrow-linewidth photonic laser meet the phase-noise and coherence requirements to drive coherent single- and two-qubit gates on trapped-ion optical qubits?
fields.limits: Coherence limited by residual laser drift and AC mains magnetic-field fluctuations; separate chips connected via fibers/free-space optics rather than full monolithic integration.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Resolved Sideband Cooling and Single Qubit Gate Performance. a Resolved sideband cooling showing $\bar{n}_{str}=0.04(4)$ of the out-of-phase motional mode (stretch mode) of two ions. b Rabi oscillations on the $\ket{S_{1/2},m_{J}=+1/2}\rightarrow\ket{D_{5/2},m_{J}=+1/2}$ transition. The ion is cooled with Doppler laser cooling, polarization gradient cooling, and resolved sideband cooling with the integrated laser. We find a total residual thermal occupation of $\bar{n}\approx 5.9(8)$ (including all motional modes) by fitting to a thermal model. c Randomized Benchmarking yields an average single qubit Clifford fidelity of $99.61\pm 0.03\%$ . For each depth, ten independently generated random Clifford sequences are measured with 100 shots each. Clifford gates are decomposed into native $\pi$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}$ rotations, with Z rotations implemented in software. The sequence depth $d$ denotes the number of Clifford gates.
fields.figure_gloss: Resolved sideband cooling, Rabi oscillations, and randomized benchmarking curve showing sequence survival fidelity as a function of Clifford gate depth $d$.

fields.result: Realized on-chip absorptive optomechanical memory for telecom-band photons operating near mechanical ground state with phonon occupancy $n_\text{th} = 0.32$ during storage and on-demand retrieval at few-photon level.
fields.question: Can an on-chip optomechanical resonator achieve absorptive quantum memory for telecom photons near the mechanical ground state with flexible on-demand retrieval?
fields.limits: Measured at 20 mK base temperature with storage operated in the few-photon regime.

fields.result: Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.
fields.question: How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?
fields.limits: Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: From bit (classical data) to qubit (quantum data). Quantum algorithm and corresponding problem inputs are compiled to concrete quantum circuits. Quantum state preparation: for classical vector $\bm{v}$ , the task is to prepare a quantum state $|\psi\rangle=\|\bm{v}\|^{-1}\sum_{j}v_{j}|j\rangle$ . QRAM: For binary vector $\bm{v}$ , the task is to construct a unitary transformation that $|j\rangle|0\rangle\rightarrow|j\rangle|v_{j}\rangle$ . Block-encoding: for matrix $A$ , the task is to construct a unitary $U_{A}$ such that $(\left\langle{0}\right|^{\otimes a}\otimes I_{n})U_{A}(\left|{0}\right\rangle^{\otimes a}\otimes I_{n})=A/\alpha$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.

fields.result: Non-reciprocal three-cavity system exhibits a third-order exceptional point from the coalescence of two second-order exceptional points, speeding up entanglement generation time to $t_m \approx 15$ ns with an enhancement factor scaling as $J^{-4/5}$.
fields.question: How do interactions between different orders of exceptional points affect entanglement dynamics and generation speed in non-reciprocally coupled quantum systems?
fields.prior: Hermitian counterpart required $t_m \approx 250$ ns to reach maximum entanglement generation time.
fields.limits: Single-excitation subspace under post-selection against decay to ground state $|0,0,0\rangle$; assumes cavity dissipation rates are matched ($\Delta\gamma/\gamma \ll 1$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Phase diagram of $\text{EP}_{2}$ and $\text{EP}_{3}$ . The upper and lower boundary curves correspond to second-order and third-order EPs, respectively. The dynamical evolution in yellow region corresponds to symmetry-unbroken phase, while the other two regions represent distinct symmetry-broken phases connected by a third-order exceptional phase transition.
fields.figure_gloss: Phase diagram over asymmetry parameter $e$ and coupling $\Omega_2$, showing boundaries for second-order exceptional points ($	ext{EP}_2$) and third-order exceptional points ($	ext{EP}_3$) separating symmetry-unbroken and broken phases.

fields.result: Rust-backed Python library Propaq matches monoprop and achieves up to $\sim 100\times$ speedup over existing packages like pauli-prop, pyrauli, and PauliPropagation.jl at $10^9$ terms. Natively supports arbitrary operator bases and hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation.
fields.question: How to implement a flexible, high-performance Heisenberg propagation package supporting arbitrary operator bases and hybrid simulation schemes?
fields.prior: Packages including pauli-prop, pyrauli, PauliPropagation.jl, and MajoranaPropagation.jl.
fields.limits: Coefficient truncation threshold of $10^{-6}$; benchmarks evaluated on 64 AMD EPYC 7H12 cores for Trotterized 2D TFIM and 2D Hubbard models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Heisenberg propagation wall-clock runtime and number of terms (inset) for various packages. Here, we benchmark computing expectation values of a $Z$ observable for (a) Trotterized time evolution of a 2D TFIM on a $6\times 6$ square lattice ( $J=1.0$ , $h=0.5$ , $\Delta t=0.1$ ) and (b) Trotterized time evolution of a 2D Hubbard model on a $3\times 3$ square lattice ( $t=1.0$ , $U=4.0$ , $\Delta t=0.1$ ). All backends use a coefficient cutoff of $10^{-6}$ and 64 threads, except for the single-threaded pauli-prop package. As shown, Propaq exceeds the performance of all packages in both bases, except for the monoprop package which is roughly equal to Propaq.
fields.figure_gloss: Propagation wall time in seconds (main plot) and number of terms (inset) versus Trotter step count for TFIM (left) and Hubbard (right) models across multiple propagation packages using 64 threads and a $10^{-6}$ coefficient cutoff.

fields.result: Cavity magnonics can be driven into non-Hermitian and quantum regimes via reservoir-mediated dissipative coupling, Floquet frequency modulation, and parametric squeezing transfer. Long-lived subradiant modes near anti-$\mathcal{PT}$ exceptional points lower the bistability threshold as $|\Omega_{\rm th}|^{2}\propto(\gamma-\Gamma)^{3}/K$, scaling quantum Fisher information as $\mathcal{F}_{Q}\propto\varepsilon^{-4}$.
fields.question: How do engineered dissipative coupling, Floquet modulation, and parametric driving enable quantum state generation, nonreciprocal transport, and enhanced sensing in cavity magnonics?
fields.limits: Dynamical stability requires parametric drive strength $x < 1$. Bright-magnon quadrature squeezing persists only below critical thermal occupation $\bar{n}_{m}^{\rm crit}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Characteristic eigenspectrum of a dissipatively coupled anti- $\mathcal{PT}$ -symmetric system. (a) Real and (b) imaginary parts of the eigenvalues as functions of the relative detuning $\delta$ . The EPs at $|\delta|=\Gamma$ separate the spectrally split regime from the regime of frequency coalescence and linewidth bifurcation into superradiant and subradiant branches. Adapted from Ref. [ 27 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Real and imaginary eigenspectrum parts plotted versus relative detuning $\delta$. At exceptional points $|\delta|=\Gamma$, real frequencies coalesce while imaginary damping rates bifurcate into superradiant and subradiant branches.

fields.result: Amplifies cross-Kerr interaction between two microwave cavity modes via single-frequency transmon drive near intermediate-state divergences, achieving on-demand $\textsc{crot}$ gate for rotation-symmetric bosonic error correction without requiring multiple frequencies or frequency-tunable elements.
fields.question: How can a direct, code-agnostic $\textsc{crot}$ gate between bosonic cavity modes be implemented in circuit QED without multi-tone driving or gigahertz frequency tuning?
fields.prior: Prior direct implementations required $>1$ GHz frequency tunability or multi-tone drives scaling with logical state size.
fields.limits: Numerical and analytical modeling. Assumes perfect cancellation of self-Kerr from auxiliary side transmons, neglecting higher-order mode distortions and unmodeled side-transmon Hilbert spaces.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: (a) Kerr spectrum (in units of the no-drive cross-Kerr) in the weak-coupling regime at fixed effective amplitude $\left|\frac{\Omega_{d}}{\delta_{d}}\right|=1$ . Dispersive structures arise from drive-induced resonances. The dashed green and blue vertical lines mark single-cavity resonances where both cross- and (unwanted) self-Kerr effects are amplified. The desired working point lies near the two-cavity resonance marked by the dashed magenta vertical line. (b) The immediate vicinity of the chosen resonance, overlaid with the numerical sixth-order terms $K_{\textrm{dis}}$ $\propto N_{a}^{2}N_{b}$ (purple) and $N_{a}N_{b}^{2}$ (brown) that lead to distortions. The gray shaded region identifies a range of drive detuning for which the higher-order distortions are mild, while the cross-Kerr coefficient already experiences significant growth close to the resonance. Our chosen crot working point is at $\delta_{d}/\alpha=0.835$ (gray vertical line). (c) Teleportation-based error-correction (EC) circuit for rotation-symmetric bosonic (RSB) codes, employing two crot gates [ crot $(2\pi/NM)$ and crot $(\pi/N^{2})$ , with $M$ and $N$ as the RSB code orders], two measurements (DP $=$ discrete-phase measurement; $\overline{X}=$ logical- $X$ measurement), and a final classically controlled single-mode gate to complete the teleportation. (Figure adapted from Ref. [ 24 ] .) (d) Wigner diagrams of input and output [after crot $(2\pi/NM)$ ] states at our chosen working point, for different loss error $k$ and phase error $\theta$ values. (e) Memory task: Ratio $R$ of the average fidelities, after EC with actual crot gates versus the unencoded physical qubit, for different loss and dephasing rates $\kappa$ and $\kappa_{\text{ph}}$ . The small black circles are numerically simulated data points; the contour plot interpolates across those points. The solid white line marks $R=1$ for EC with actual crot gates; the dashed white line gives the analogous line for EC with ideal crot s.
fields.figure_gloss: Effective self- and cross-Kerr nonlinearities plotted against drive detuning at fixed drive strength $\left|\Omega_d/\delta_d\right|=1$, showing resonant divergences that enhance cross-Kerr interaction while distinguishing two-cavity from single-cavity resonances.

fields.result: Constructs bosonic four-body matrix-quantum-mechanics potentials via Floquet-engineered oscillating two-body spin interactions with a constant number of unitaries per cycle. Control-frequency bandwidth scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$ with matrix size $N$, reaching non-perturbative couplings $\lambda \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ at driving frequencies $\omega \sim \mathcal{O}(\text{MHz})$.
fields.question: Can four-body potentials of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics be simulated on an analog optical-lattice platform without the deep circuits of digital implementations?
fields.limits: Requires non-spin-conserving spin-spin interactions and large-spin ferromagnetic regime ($m \sim j$). Bosonic Hilbert space must be truncated.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : This plot shows the convergence of the spin model to the truncated $SU(2)\times SO(2)$ bosonic matrix model (with $\lambda=2$ ) for the ground state energy. For both models, we have chosen the truncation $\Lambda=6$ . The relative error for $j=3$ is $0.5\,\%$ and improves to $0.007\,\%$ for $j=200$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Ground-state energy convergence as a function of spin size $j$ comparing the large-spin model against the truncated $SU(2) \times SO(2)$ bosonic matrix model with $\lambda=2$ and cutoff $\Lambda=6$. Relative error is $0.5\,\%$ at $j=3$ and drops to $0.007\,\%$.

fields.result: Constructs transversal distributed logical fanout and global controlled-$Z$ ($GCZ$) operations across encoded code blocks to minimize non-local communication and entanglement overhead.
fields.question: How can logical fanout operations across remote nodes in distributed quantum computers be implemented fault-tolerantly with reduced non-local communication overhead?
fields.limits: Theoretical and architectural analysis; illustrated specifically on Bivariate Bicycle code blocks.

fields.result: Even-distance Generalized Superfast Encoding maintains constant stabilizer weights of 4 or 6, exhibiting a quantum memory pseudo-threshold crossing near physical depolarizing error rate $p \approx 4\times 10^{-3}$.
fields.question: Can a fermion-to-qubit mapping achieve fault-tolerant quantum memory with threshold-like error suppression under circuit-level noise?
fields.prior: Generalized Superfast Encoding was restricted to error detection or odd-distance constructions with weight-6 stabilizers (Brown et al. 2024), with no fault-tolerant quantum memory threshold observed.
fields.limits: Circuit-level depolarizing noise simulations only; evaluated on two code instances ($[[48,8,6]]$ and $[[64,8,8]]$); requires $N > d$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical depolarizing error rate $p$ , for the $[\![48,8,6]\!]$ and $[\![64,8,8]\!]$ even-weight GSE codes, decoded with Relay-BP using AlphaSyndrome-scheduled syndrome extraction. Solid curves are log-log power-law fits to each code’s data. The dashed line is the unencoded (physical) error rate for reference. The higher-distance code suppresses logical error more strongly at low $p$ with the two curves approaching each other near $p\approx 4\times 10^{-3}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical error rate $p$. The $[[64,8,8]]$ code suppresses errors faster than the $[[48,8,6]]$ code below their projected crossing point near $p \approx 4\times 10^{-3}$.

fields.result: Asymmetric $(5,3)$ quantum parity code with 15 physical qubits matches the optimization performance of the symmetric $(5,5)$ code requiring 25 qubits because QAOA objective degrades significantly more under bit flips than phase flips.
fields.question: How do asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise channels affect QAOA performance across different circuit decompositions, and can asymmetric quantum error correction exploit this asymmetry?
fields.limits: Simulated on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment problem; syndrome extraction circuit noise and gate-level QEC fault-tolerance overhead not directly modeled in the QEC evaluation.
tools: Layer-level and gate-level Pauli noise models
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: The performance of the QAOA algorithm when using different sizes of the outer and inner repetition code of the quantum parity code, $(m_{1},m_{2})$ . The lower $\Delta$ the better. The shown plot corresponds to layer level noise for $d=2$ layers and similar plots can be drawn for the other cases considered above. The (5, 5) code beats the standard 9-qubit Shor code (3, 3) , but due to the asymmetric effect of the noise on the cost function, the (5, 3) code suffices to achieve the same results. Lines only guide the eye. The visible numerical inaccuracies are inherited from our numerical simulation, see section IV.3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Residual cost deviation $\Delta$ plotted against physical error probability $p$ under $d=2$ layer-level noise for uncoded QAOA and various quantum parity code configurations $(n_1,n_2)$.

fields.result: Solving the ECDLP on $\mathtt{secp256k1}$ requires 19,397 physical trapped-ion qubits and 25.7 days for a 63% success probability per attempt, executing $40\cdot 10^6$ Toffoli gates over 1457 logical qubits.
fields.question: How many physical qubits and how much runtime does a fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computer need to compute 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithms under realistic noise, transport, and loss constraints?
fields.prior: Prior trapped-ion estimates required 1.2 million to 9.4 million physical qubits; recent generic-architecture estimates needed $60\cdot 10^6$ Toffolis (Schrottenloher 2026).
fields.limits: Assumes physical two-qubit gate error rate $p = 10^{-4}$, single-qubit error rate $10^{-5}$, swap-loss with $p_{\mathrm{leak}} = p/10$ and $p_{\mathrm{loss}} = p/1000$. Success probability lower-bounded assuming all 69 memory blocks remain active throughout full runtime.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5 : Full-scale $\mathtt{secp256k1}$ device. Purple blocks are magic-state factories required for $\mathrm{CCZ}$ state generation, green blocks are memory blocks, orange blocks are cat-state factories, and blue blocks are Bell-state bundles for LM2 measurements. Each group of four orange blocks forms a mobile cat-state bundle pair. The two cyan sites inside each magic-factory group are local six-qubit C6 Bell-state sources. The cobalt and crimson blocks are reserved for two Logical CliNR instances used for Clifford-frame clearing. The small gray box attached to each code block is its local ion reservoir, while the full loading reservoir runs along the right edge of the device.
fields.figure_gloss: Physical layout of the 19,397-qubit $\mathtt{secp256k1}$ processor, showing 69 memory blocks, 4 CCZ magic-state factories, edge-packed cat-state factories, and Bell-state routing channels.

fields.result: Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.
fields.question: How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?
fields.limits: Analytical and numerical compilation models; assumes single-pulse error rates $p \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$, readout error $p_m \approx 0.01$, and $T_2 \approx 19.3\ \mu\text{s}$.
tools: surface code QEC / lattice surgery error modeling
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: QFT resource estimate. (a) Pulse count scaling comparing linear Parity Twine QFT (red) with the reference Fowler QFT implementation (blue) as a function of device length $L$ . Both implementations scale quadratically. The inset shows the pulse count ratio of Twine/Fowler with more than 22% asymptotic reduction in pulse count for Parity Twine QFT. (b) Circuit depth scaling comparing both QFT implementations for increasing exclusion radii $r$ . (c) Depth ratio of Twine/Fowler indicating more than 50% reduction for parallel pulse operation while the reduction is less pronounced for finite exclusion radii.
fields.figure_gloss: Physical exchange-pulse count and Twine/Fowler pulse count ratio as a function of device length $L$ for the quantum Fourier transform.

fields.result: Ancilla-mediated inter-block logical $R_{ZZ}$ gate enables multi-block $[[4,2,2]]$ error detection for QAOA Max-Cut. Encoded circuits maintain higher ground-state probability than unencoded baselines up to noise rate $p = 0.03$ under grid-routed two-qubit depolarizing noise and up to $p = 0.04$ with all-to-all connectivity.
fields.question: How can multi-block $[[4,2,2]]$ error detection be implemented for QAOA Max-Cut circuits using non-transversal inter-block two-qubit rotations?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation on a single 4-vertex cycle graph $C_4$. Post-selection acceptance rate drops exponentially with circuit depth and error rates.
